And, so far as I am concerned, I feel it my duty -and I am sincere and honest in this,-I feel that I am voicing the feeling of my constituency from one end to the other- to criticise and oppose this tariff brought down by the Minister of Finance.
Let us come to close quarters on the question as to whether or not these proposals are necessary to raise a revenue for
	i
Canada's participation in the war. Let us face the issue fairly and squarely. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has said that $6,000,000 are necessary for the payment of interest on the $150,000,000 and that $3,000,000 are necessary to form the nucleus of a pension fund; a total of $9,000,000. The Minister of Finance says further that an additional revenue of $40,000,000 will be raised by the imposition of these taxes. Will some hon. gentleman on the other side of the House show me how the $31,000,000 are going to be used for war purposes? The Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke to-day as if there were some secret in connection with the disposition of this amount. If there are other purposes for which these $31,000,000 are going to be used, why does not the Government take gentlemen on this side of the House into their confidence? What is the use of telling us that $40,000,000 are absolutely necessary to carry on the war so far as Canada is concerned when the greatest necessity hon. gentlemen can show is that of $6,000,000 for interest and $3,000,000 for pension fund? Where is the remainder going? I repeat that I invite some hon. gentleman on the other side of the House to show me in what way these $31,000,000 are going to be used for war purposes.
The first of the three ways in which the Finance Minister expects to raise additional revenue is the imposition of special taxes upon banks, trust companies and certain insurance companies. I am perfectly in accord with the Minister of Finance in the matter of a tax for war purposes-or for the raising of any legitimate revenue-upon banks, trust and loan companies and insurance companies. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House tell us that tne big interests, the big corporations, the wealthy people of this country, are the people who are going to pay these extra taxes. I think I can show them that that is not the fact. Banks, trust companies and insurance companies are the only corporations that are taxed; they are the only wealthy people who are subjected to taxation. Does the Finance Minister propose to tax telegraph and cable companies? He does not. He says that every telegram originating in Canada shall bear a tax of so many cents, and he gives the companies authority to charge the additional toll and to collect the same from the person sending the telegram. Why does he not impose a tax upon telegraph and cable companies?
Then we come to the railway companies. If there is one class of corporation in this country that might fairly be taxed; if there-

is one class of corporation that has been waxing rich at the expense of this country, it is the railway corporation. Against railway corporations I have nothing to say; they are doing great good; they are helping to develop the country. But in such a time of stress as this, when, as my hon. friend says, the rich interests of Canada are being taxed, why are the railway companies subjected to not one cent of extra taxation? It is true that every purchaser of a berth in a railway car, every purchaser of a chair in^ a parlour car and every purchaser of a railway ticket must pay a tax. I do not complain about that; if I have any fault to find it is that the minister should have exempted purchasers of second-class tickets from this tax, because, as a general rule, they are not able to pay. But has it occurred to the Minister of Finance that the railways go scot free in this matter? The same applies to steamship and steamboat companies. Any one buying a steamboat ticket must pay an extra tax into the treasury; against that I do not object. But has it occurred to the friends of the Minister of Finance that the steamboat companies, many of which are heavily subsidized by the Government, are not paying one cent into the Canadian treasury by way of extra taxation? Let it not be heard again, then, that the big corporations and the rich people of Canada are bearing the brunt of this special taxation.
I am perfectly in accord with the imposition of a stamp tax on checks, receipts and deposit receipts. As to the extra rate on letters and post cards, I do not think that will be burdensome to the people, but I would rather see the Minister of Finance go back to the time previous to 1896 when we had a three-cent rate, which would not be so inconvenient to the people as the proposed method.
I wish to point out that proprietary and patent medicine is the only article of commerce which bears a stamp tax. Proprietary and patent medicines are subject to an increased tariff of 7i and 5 per cent, and in addition must hear a stamp tax which will amount in the aggregate to a very large sum. I do not think that this is quite fair; the Minister of Finance went far enough when he proposed a 7i rate upon proprietary and patent medicines coming into Canada. I have received many protests by telegram and letter against this proposed stamp tax, and I hope that the minister, before he brings down the Bill which will crystalize these proposals into
legislation, will consider the' advisability of making a change in his proposals so far as proprietary and patent medicines are concerned. On every bottle or package which costs ten cents or less the tax will be one cent, and one cent for each ten cents of retail price.	I think that goes too
far. Public opinion has been directed *against patent medicines manufacturers and dealers,	hut I think that we
are now getting a better class of patent medicines than we were getting in years past. They are, after all, medicines which the poor man uses extensively. If he goes to the doctor to get something for his cold or bronchitis, the doctor will charge him one or two dollars, and in addition he will have to go to the drug store and pay for medicine. But if he goes to the drug store in the first place, he gets the patent medicine without paying doctor's fees, and in some cases his distress is relieved just as effectively as if he had obtained a prescription from the doctor.
There is some doubt as to whether or not this stamp tax will increase the revenue of the country. I think it has already been pointed out that in 1896, the year in which the late Conservative Administration went out of power, the then Finance Minister, now the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), was approached by delegations with a view to the introduction of an imperial penny postage rate of two cents ; but in his Budget speech of 1896 the hon. gentleman referred to the subject in this way:
i
There is now a deficit of nearly $800,000 between the total receipts and total expenditures from post office services and this I fear makes the time somewhat distant when what otherwise might be fairly asked for might be granted, that is a reduction upon postage rates in this country.
What happened? In June of the same year-the Budget was delivered in April- my right hon. friend who now leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) led the Liberal forces in this country to success and formed a Government. In 1897, or possibly in 1896, Mr. Mulock, now Sir William Mulock, the then Postmaster General, introduced the imperial penny postage. In 1896. when the then Finance Minister said they could not afford to give reduced rates of postage, what was the condition of the Post Office Department? In that year they had a deficit of over $800,000; but from the time the imperial penny postage was introduced by Sir William Mulock there were surplusses in the Post Office Depart-
Has the price of raw wool advanced very much owing to the war?

I presume that it has. I thought my hon. friend was going to ask a question about the gummed slip. I am meeting the arguments advanced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his friends behind him, that the manufacturers of this country would not take advantage of the increase of duties to unduly enhance the prices of their manufactured goods. Had I time I would go into the question of the manufacture into the finished product of the raw material imported into this country, and consider how much manufacturers of underwear for example, are entitled to get after paying the increased duty on wool and other raw material; but I presume that somebody else will take up that question. To continue: at that very time also the Ideal Bedding Company, of Toronto, makers of brass and iron beds, wire mattresses, spring beds, institution beds, cots, cribs, steel couch beds, mixed and felt mattresses, etc., issued the following letter from Toronto, dated February 26, 1915:
Gentlemen,.-We thank you for your order of the 22nd instant, and take pleasure in entering same at our present prices as indicated in circular letter which was sent out to you recently.
Our price list is now under revision and will be issued early in March. Owing to tariff changes, prices will be advanced ranging from 5 to 12 i per cent.
So that this manufacturing firm is not charitably disposed towards the consumers
of this country; and they do not hide the fact, for they say in language bold and plain that their increase will be from 5 to 12J per cent, and that it is due to the tariff changes. I have another circular in my hand, dated February 15, 1915, issued oy Staunton's, Limited. It is headed, " Notice of Advance in Prices," and says:
Dear Sir,-Please note that on August 28th last, we were forced to advance prices on certain patterns as per particulars noted hereunder. Since that date all orders have been booked at the new figures which will apply also to all repeat orders you may send to us.
In view of the still further advances in cost of manufacture, due to the new war duties and taxes, we may be forced to make other changes in prices and have to notify you that all prices are subject to change without notice.
And then he gives a lot of figures apparently about wall paper, so I suppose this firm is in the paper manufacturing industry. In addition to that, I have had placed in my hands a communication from a retail dealer in one of the maritime provinces stating that between March 1 and March 15, he would advance the price of boots and shoes by 5 per cent, and rubbers by from 5 to 10 per cent. That is another instance of how charitably disposed the manufacturers are to the consumers of this country.
As I have said, if some hon. gentlemen opposite can show me that this $40,000,000 which the Finance Minister proposes to raise by his new taxation is going to be devoted to war purposes, I will withdraw every word I have said against these taxes. But this money is not going for war purposes. The very extreme limit, as was pointed out by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, is $9,000,000; $6,000,000 for interest, but perhaps that was a trifle low, and $3,000,000 for the nucleus of a pension fund. That makes $9,000,000. What is going to become of the other $31,000,000? It is going to be used to make up the deficit of the present Administration; and there is no use denying that fact. Hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken of extravagance and reckless expenditure. The Minister of Finance told us that the late Administration had left a burden upon his shoulders. He said: it is true that when we came into power we found some money in the treasury, but very many liabilities. Well, Mr. Speaker, the only distinction I can see between the administration of the two parties is that now there is no money in the treasury, and very many more liabilities. And what is the cause? Let any man in this country sit down for just a moment

and, consider that the Liberal Government from 1897 down to 1911 could meet all the ordinary expenses of this country and have no deficit, whereas it took the gentlemen who now control the destinies of this country only three years to make a change in all that. That is something which the people of this country should consider, and we are here to assist them in solving that problem.	.
Let us look at the Public. Accounts. On pages 20 and 21 of the Public Accounts for the year ended March 31, 1914, it is shown that during the extraordinary period of expansion between 1896 and 1911, when the Laurier Government was in power and Mr. Fieldjng Minister of Finance, the increased expenditure chargeable to consolidated fund was never greater than $8,000,000 in any one year. The ordinary expenditure of the Laurier Government during the last four years was as follows: In 1908, $76,641,000; in 1909, $84,064,000; in 1910, $79,411,000; and in 1911, $87,740,000. The Conservative Government came into power in 1911, and became responsible for the expenditure of the year ended March 31, 1913. If there was extravagance in the Estimates brought down by Mr. Fielding in 1911, that was the time for my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce to strike his pen through those Estimates and to reduce the extravagance which he said existed under the former Government. If there was extravagance under the late Government it existed more in the year 1911 than before that time, and yet the present Government instead of cutting down the Estimates prepared by Mr. Fielding in	1911 presented them to
this House in the session of 1912, and passed	them item by item.
In 1912 the expenditure on Consolidated Revenue Fund Account was $98,161,000, in 1913 it went up to $112,059,000, and in 1914 it reached the great sum of $127,384,000. If it was extravagance on the part of the Liberal Government in 1911 to expend $87,000,000 is there any word in the dictionary-and if there is the Minister of Finance will find it because he is an expert in using extravagant adjectives-which would adequately describe the extravagance of this Government in 1914 when it expended $127,000,000? The Minister of Finance estimates that on March 31, 1915, the expenditure will be $140,000,000, that it will require the same sum for the financial year 1916. The question naturally arises as to whether this Government has done as much for the people of thia country

through this huge expenditure as was done by their predecessors in office with a much less expenditure? I do not believe it has. If the prediction of the Finance Minister comes true that he will get $40,000,000 from this extra taxation then it will mean an additional tax of $6.14 on every man, woman and child in Canada. The Government expects to get from this extra taxation $31,000,000 which most undoubtedly does not go for war purposes, and even then tney will be in the hoie some $50,000,000. Let us look at where those additional expenditures went. Surely there is not a 'man on either side who will say that there was not more railway construction in Canada between 1904 and 1912 than there has been spent since but let me contrast the expenditure by the Liberal and Conservative Governments, on railway subsidies. During their fifteen years in power the Liberals granted railway subsidies totalling $25,140,000, and then tne party of retrenchment came in and during the three years 1912, 1913 and 1914 they granted railway subsidies totalling $24,830,000, or almost as much in three years as was spent on this account during the fifteen years of the Liberal Government. There is at least one item among the railway subsidies granted by the present Government for which no defence can be offered and that is the subsidy to the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway Company, an Ontario government-owned railway, a railway built and operated by the Ontario Government and which at tne time was paying good dividends. To this railway the Conservative 'Government doled out subsidies aggregating about $2,000,000 and I defy any man in this House to defend that transaction.
There [DOT] has been considerable discussion in this House as to the advisability of the great increase in the Civil Service of this country, but no one has been able to make out that the work of the country has developed with such immeasurable strides during the past three years that it requires 10,000 civil servants more than we had in 1911. Certainly the people from the part of the country from which I come have the idea that this Government is not doing as much for the people as their predecessors did, and they fail to understand how it requires an addition of 10,000 more civil .servants to man the public offices.
I would not perhaps so much blame the Government for their extravagance since 1911 under ordinary conditions, but we have been told in this debate, and we were told by the Prime Minister in 1912, that war

with Germany was imminent. He told us that be heard the thunder of the guns, and that he saw the war clouds on the horizon and Germany in conflict against Great Britain and her Allies. Endowed *with such foresight, was not that the time for the right hon. gentleman to take to retrenchment and put an end to extravagance? To-day the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the war came suddenly as a thunderbolt from the sky, but the Prime Minister told us that he *saw it coming three years ago, and I leave these two gentlemen to reconcile their difference between themselves. Before the Conservative Government came into power in 1911 the Prime Minister isaid that the increase in what is known as ordinary controllable expenditure from $36,000,000 in 1896 to $87,000,000 in 1907 was proof of extravagance beyond any possible defence. If the right hon. gentleman was in earnest in making that statement he. should have bridled the extravagance of bis Government when it came to power, but he did nothing of the kind. It is clear that he made no effort to control the extravagance and unbridled expenditure of his Government.
There are a few other observations I wish to make before closing. My hon. friend from South Toronto (Me. Maedonell), in replying to my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), isaid that the labour men of this country were favourable to the proposals of the Minister of Finance in his Budget. I do not pretend to know what authority the hon. member had to make that statement. He probably had the authority of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association; but he certainly did not have the authority of the labour people of this country. With the prices of foodstuffs and the price of clothing going up, as I can prove by letters of manufacturers, with unemployment and hard times, with the trades-people of this country working only half time, it cannot reasonably be expected that they will bow down and say: burden us up some more, Mr. Minister of Finance; it is true that we are making only half the money that we were making more than three years ago; but go ahead, we can stand more burdens to-day with one dollar than we could then with two dollars. I do not believe that the hon. member for South Toronto had any authority to speak for the labouring people of this country. I do not believe that they are in favour of these proposals in so far as "taxation on foodstuffs
and clothing is concerned, and I do not blame them for not agreeing to the motion.
There is no class of people more anxious and willing to pay the legitimate demands of taxation than the miners and steel workers and fishermen of Nova Scotia. They ire willing to pay those taxes and to undergo those burdens when they have the capacity to do so; but is it fair to ask them and other similarly situated labourers throughout the length and breadth of this land to pay an increased taxation, ranging from 5 per c-ent to 12 per cent, on the bite of food they eat and on the mite of clothing they put on their bodies, when they are earning half the wages that they earned three years ago? The 'labouring people of this country are not going to stand for such a thing. We are told: oh, the farmers of the West are reaping benefits from this war; they are getting handsome prices for their wheat. The moment they get those prices, the Minister of Finance comes around with a hat and says: Mr. Farmer, you are getting an enhanced price for your wheat on account of the war, and you must contribute a portion of'your profits to the Government. He increases the taxes to all the consumers of this country; but he lets the railway and cable and telegraph corporations and the great steamboat companies of the country go without one bit of taxation.

No passing of the hat
with him; he takes a club.

I was putting it mildly. As far as voting the $150,000,000 for war purposes to assist the Motherland concerned, there is no dissentient voice on this side of the House. The Minister of Trade and Commerce need not plead with us; he need not tell us what'the result of this war has been on the commerce of this country in order to get us to vote this money. We will vote it freely and we are willing to vote twice as much if necessary; but we call a halt when the people of this country are asked to be taxed $31,000,000 over and above what is necessary to carry on the war.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite, in the press and on the floor of the House, seek to spread the idea that we on this side of the House are not patriotic, that we are not loyal to the Motherland. I am not going to use much breath in combatting that idea. All I can say is that many of us have sent our brothers or our sons to the front, and that they are now fighting in the trenches in defence of that Motherland. Surely it is weakness on the part of any public man or

of any newspaper in this country to cast aspersions and slurs at my right hon. friend and the people who support him and the people who are so loyally supporting the Government in voting this $150,000,000. There is in this' country a class of politicians that I would like to call political snipers, who, so to speak, are trying to 9 p.m. bring down the reputation for patriotism and loyalty that has always characterized my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Statements have appeared in the press and circulars have been sent out of this House, at least to one constituency of which I know in the province of Manitoba, to impress upon this country that we, the Liberal party, headed by our right hon. leader, are against doing anything for the Motherland. I would like to number amongst those political snipers and to make their chieftain the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler). At a meeting held a day or two ago in the city of Ottawa, he made this remark, which is worthy of the hon. gentleman :
He said that Hon. Hr. JBeland, who is now a pr soner in Belgium, did not go to Belgium to take part in the war, but to get a wife. If he had b en in Canada when the war broke out, he might and might not have volunteered to go to the front.
I acknowledge that I am a partisan; but I think that no hon. gentleman on this side of the House and that very few hon. gentlemen on the other side would get up in a public meeting in the city of Ottawa or elsewhere and make such a remark about a political adversary as was made by the hon. member foT Kings and Albert. Dr. Beland is to-day a prisoner of war, captured by the Germans. Previous to that he was made a lieutenant-colonel by the hon. Minister of Militia. No one knows better than the hon. Minister of Militia and few know better than my hon. friend the member for Kings and Albert that, if Dr. Beland had not been captured, he wfiuld to-day have been giving relief to the stricken people of Belgium and to the stricken soldiers of Great Britain and her allies. I speak of this only to show how small some people can become when they want to create an unfavourable impression against their political opponents. Let us hope that those Canadian political snipers will have the same effect in lowering the esteem for my right hon. leader amongst the people of this country as the German snipers will have in lowering the

prestige and power of Great Britain in the trenches of Flanders.
We are voting $150,000,000 towards helping our Motherland to carry on this war. This Government would be well advised if it would take into consideration and put into effect some system whereby it could at the present time give some aid to the stricken Belgians. Perhaps we in this country do not appreciate what the little Belgian army has done for us. Perhaps we do not appreciate that at Liege the Belgian army saved France, and by saving France saved England, and by saving England saved Canada from the impress of Prussian militarism. Belgium could have made a formal protest against the breach of her neutrality by the German forces. She would not have lessened her honour amongst the nations of the world by doing so, because she was scarcely large enough to do anything more formidable than that. She chose, without a moment's hesitation, the nobler part, and sent her little bands of soldiers to confront the hordes of oncoming Germans. She held them at bay for weeks, until France was able to recruit her army and England was ready for action. Had it not been for this, few of us can comprehend what might have happened in this world before this time. France would have been crushed; Russia would have been overcome before she had had time to mobilize, and the British Empire, perhaps, left to fight a lone struggle for existence. But she did all this at awful sacrifice to herself. Her cities were ravaged, her cornfields destroyed, her women and children killed. To-day she is getting some little assistance from Canadians individually. In Nova Scotia we carried on a movement to send supplies and clothing to the stricken Belgians. But individual effort cannot do for Belgians all that Canada can do for them. We have an organized Government, and I hope we have unlimited credit. I believe the Government would be well advised if, in voting this $100,000,000, they would add $1,000,000 or $2,000,000-and borrow it in the old land if necessary-to assist the Belgians and to procure for them food and clothing. I simply throw out this hint. I will vote for such an appropriation as gladly and cordially as I will vote for the passing of the hundred million dollars.
Mr. JOSEPH A. DESCARRIES (Jacques-Cartier) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, for a new member to rise for the first time in this House and address his fellow-inembers is always a-solemn moment. For that reason

my thanks are due my honourable friends for their-so kind reception, and their applause is for me an encouragement.
True it is, Mr. Speaker, that I am,one of the youngest members of this House, but bygone years have already left their snows on my head, and on such an occasion, I must not allow shyness to get the best of me. My plain task is to perform my duty as member for the beautiful and important riding of Jacques-Cartier, the electors of which have sent me here as their representative.
At the outset, I must be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to recall with deep feeling the memory of the statesman, of the distinguished gentleman, who was the ex-minister of Public Works, the Hon. Mr. Monk, who had been given by the electors of Jacques-Cartier a mandate, which at their request I am here to. continue. The genial manners, the talent and the love of study which were characteristic of the ex-minister are still remembered by all the hon. members. A single word may typify his whole career: he was a man who kept faith.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is as representative of Jacques-Cartier, that I intend to enter into the debate which has engaged the attention of the House during four long weeks, on the subject of the budget, as laid down in the speech of the Hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. White). Before and up to that speech, there seemed to exist an admirable consensus of opinion between the two great parties that face each other in this House.
Last August a special session of Parliament was called, and there prevailed the most perfect harmony. The members on both sides were at one in their enthusiasm to vote the budget submitted for their approval, a budget rendered necessary by the war, to enable aid to be sent, on behalf of Canada, to the British Empire.
What then has happened since that day to break the political truce between the two parties? Has the Hon. the Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes) wasted the lives of Canada's youth, of the soldiers sent to the defence of the Empire? Have the moneys voted by the House been diverted from their object? Nothing of the sort has been alleged, but on the contrary flattering expressions of approval have been bestowed on the Hon. the Minister of Militia. His ardour in the performance of his task has been praised and wonder has been expressed at his success, in, within a few weeks, raising almost a whole army which was sent to France and England to aid in repelling the enemy intent on conquering first Belgium and then France, the French Canadian's original motherland.
Our soldiers on the battle line have excited the admiration of old veterans for Canadian courage and valour.
What then is the reason of it all? Our friends on the other side of the House, while protesting loudly their patriotism and their desire to assist the Motherland, are profuse and bitter in their complaints against the Government. They have been seized with a hankering for power in the very turmoil of the war. At a time when Great Britain has need of our assistance, and tne Administration must dispose of all its forces, these gentlemen are attempting to storm the fortress of Government, and get into power. To obtain their end, they censure the Government who, they claim, intend to impose on the people oppressive taxation while providing for little revenue, And instead of fostering trade with Great Britain, the Government hampers it by an increase in the preferential tariff. According to their contention, patriotism is unknown in the ministerial ranks, and the Opposition have a monopoly of enthusiasm. The Government seemingly has done nothing and its overthrow has become a necessity.
What arguments are put forth in support of their views? They may be summarized in a few words: First of all, there is no necessity for further taxation. Our present revenue would be sufficient to meet the required expenditure, had not the Conservative Government been spending so lavishly. Put a stop to all this extravagance; let the expenditure be cut down and equilibrium will be restored between revenue and expenditure. Such is their first argument. The second is that our financial difficulties are not the result of the war. The third is that the new method of taxation proposed by the Government is based neither on justice nor on scientific principles. Fourthly, these gentlemen contend that there should be no increase in the preferential tariff favouring Great Britain.
As a young member, it is not my part to search the records of this House in order to furnish all the details and figures in regard to this question. It -will be sufficient for me to outline in a general way my views on the few points which I have raised. Is the Government guilty of extravagance? So these gentlemen claim, but is it a fact? It

COMMONS!
is the people's right to enquire into the truth of this statement and it is the right of the people's representatives to find out if the Government has really been prodigal of the public money as is asserted by these gentlemen. If the Government has thus been lavish, it should not be kept in power. Let us therefore examine if such is the case.
What heritage have the Liberals left behind them when they had to relinquish the reins of power? Had not indeed their successors to face thousands of millions of obligations, both direct and indirect? And first what of the Transcontinental Railway? That section from Moncton to Winnipeg was to cost only $60,000,000 and, as stated by the hon. leader of the Opposition only $13,000,000 if only the interest were taken into account. Now, this railway alone has cost at least $200,000,000. Nor is that all. Has not the Liberal Government guaranteed bonds to the extent of $125,000,000? They say we have been extravagant. But in 1896, when our political opponents came into power, has not the hon. leader of the Opposition, who is in the same position to-day, been heard to exclaim in this House and before the people, when the public expenditure amounted to only about $40,000,000, that it was extravagant? Then, addressing the people and the members of this House, did he not say: Put us into power; give us an opportunity of governing the country and the cost of the public administration will be reduced by $3,000,000. Now, what happened? In a few years, the Liberals had increased the annual expenditure to nearly $100,000,000.
Is the increase in the expenditure a sufficient reason to charge the Government with extravagance? If such is the case and such is their reasoning, then it spells the condemnation of the late Government's policy. But an imputation of that kind requires for its justification something more than a bare statement: it must be proven to be well founded. It must be shown in what case there has been extravagance, what retrenchment should have been made, what particular item was unnecessary. Now, none of the members opposite has shown that to be the case. Has any one even attempted to do so? No, Mr. Speaker.
The Conservative Administration is taxed with extravagance; but how comes it that during the three years of Conservative rule a greater surplus was realized by this Government than was ever shown by any previous Administration. In 1911-1912, the sur-

plus was $38,000,000; in 1912-1913, $56,000,000; in 1913-1914, $36,000,000: a total in round numbers of $130,000,000 in three years.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the previous Liberal Government had dug an abyss. During these same years, from 1912 to 1915, the Conservatives had to pay, for undertakings of the Liberal regime, the following sums: for the Transcontinental Railway, $56,000,000; for the Hudson Bay Railway, $9,000,000; for the Quebec bridge, $10,000,000. These amounts make up a total of $75,000,000. Nor is that all: to make up for the deficiency in the price realized on the sale of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, $5,000,000; for the purchase of the debentures of the Grand Trunk Pacific, $33,000,000; to complete the line, $15,000,000.
We are called extravagant: but who has been guilty of extravagance, Mr. Speaker? Let us consider the national debt from the 30th of September, 1911, to the 31st of July, 1914. Under the present Administration there was an increase of the national debt of only 8 millions. Before the year 1911, during a period covering two years and a few months, that is during the same length of time, the national debt under the Liberal regime was increased by 70 millions. These gentlemen sitting on your left, Mr. Speaker, allege extravagance on the part of the Government. What are the facts? In 1914-15, the estimates amounted to 210 millions; in 1915-16, to 180 millions, a saving of 30 millions. No extravagance there surely!
Now, Mr. Speaker, what do we hear on all sides, and repeated by all the members of this House? Hard times! lack of employment ! Are we not bound to provide work for the poor people? But do the Liberals, who so loudly bemoan the fate of these unfortunates; who express their pity at the sight of closed factories; who say that trade is stagnant, and money scarce; do these Liberals pretend that the time is opportune' to put a stop to all public works? Yet if the Government listen to them, 22 millions-that is the figure mentioned by Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier-22 millions of these public works, such as post offices, customs houses, drill halls, etc., will be cut off. Why! take those cities which boast of a progressive and enlightened civic administration. How do they cope with hard times? Do not their endeavours tend to provide their labouring citizens with the means of earning their living and that of their families? Do they not appropriate as large a portion as possible of the municipal funds to public undertakings that will

provide work for their unemployed? Is this indeed the time to cast doubts on Canada's future? Is this the time to stop the country in its progress? Are not its resources truly extraordinary? I say that a wise government should, during years of distress, exert itself to the utmost of its power, and through the carrying out of public works, provide employment for those who cannot secure it elsewhere. But such is not apparently the policy of our Liberal friends. The hon. leader of the Opposition himself would cut off $22,000,000 of the money intended for such public buildings as post offices, customs houses, drill halls, scattered throughout the country and giving employment to a large number of workingmen. He says these works in small towns and in different places ought to be stopped. On the other hand, the hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Martin), mayor of Montreal, would have the doors of the Dominion treasury thrown wide open and money supplied him by the bushel to provide food for the unemployed of his city, a strange contradiction indeed which cannot be explained except by these gentlemen's eagerness to reach power.
The Government has cut doifrn the expenses of legislation, immigration, railways and canals, harbours, naval service, crown lands and various other branches of the public administration.
I say it is the Liberal party that has shown extravagance while on the contrary the present Administration is endeavouring with the utmost prudence and wisdom to lead the country through these times of stress to progress and prosperity.
It is claimed, Mr. Speaker, that the war has nothing to do with the financial difficulties we have to face. I say that by itself is sufficient proof that our hon. friends on the other side of the House are not to be taken seriously and that their sole aim is to embarrass in every possible way this Government. They say there is a deficit of $60,000,000 in 1914-15, and they predict another deficit of $80,000,000 for 1915-16, besides the war expenditure which will amount to $150,000,000. The war, they say, cannot account for the excess of $140,000,000 of the expenses over the revenue. But if the war is not the cause of this deficit, how is it that it is during war time that the first deficit appears, since up to that time we have recorded the largest surpluses of all Administrations. This argument is but child's talk. Look up the customs receipts during the one year of 1914-15 and you will see a 65
decrease of $32,000,000. And the same as to all other sources of income. How could it be otherwise? The world's commerce has been stopped by the war and Canada's trade would not be affected! To think this possible is absurd ! Indeed! But for the English which has kept the trade routes opened, whereat should we be? Industry is paralysed and it is barely kept alive by orders occasioned by the war. Could the Minister of Finance have remedied this evil? No. His policy is the best possible; he has entered into an agreement with the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, whereby the necessary funds to cover the war expenditure are supplied to Canada at the same rate as that paid by Great Britain herself. And in order to allay the effect of the war on the Canadian exchequer, the Minister of Finance suggested new duties and taxes, and this is nothing to wonder at, Mr. Speaker; when, even the United States have to devise a war tariff to provide for a diminished revenue. But it is on that ground of taxation, that hon. gentlemen on the other side have based their attacks. Their contention is that the system of taxation as proposed is neither equitable nor scientifically justifiable. To prove this, the ex-prime minister of Canada forsakes his customary dignity and stoops to the expedients of the demagogue. Speaking on the special tax to be imposed on railway tickets, he caters to the lower instincts of the populace. He draws a picture Of the sumptuousness of Pullman cars. He tries to excite against the rich the envy and covetousness of the poor. In his description the children of the wealthy are without feelings, without patriotism, unable to earn a cent by their own efforts, passing through life careless, heedless, with only one thought: to live in affluence at the expense of the poor people oppressed by their greedy parents. And why this diatribe? Because the Minister of Finance proposed a tax of five cents on railway tickets. Passengers in Pullman cars pay for their seats and their berths besides paying the five cents which are paid equally by all passengers. There is not a great difference in this country between first and second class passengers and if a higher tax were imposed on first class tickets, it would fall equally on persons of medium means. But, it is stated again, your tariff is not designed to increase the revenue but to benefit the privileged and wealthy classes. In the terms of the hon. leader of the Opposition, it is framed to raise a minimum of



revenue with a maximum of hardships and losses for the country at large. It is again the struggle between protection and free-trade.
Harping always on the same chord, the hon. leader of the Opposition alleges that under the tariff a duty is imposed on the necessaries of life. Why, does he ask, tax articles which are not imported? A duty is put on spirituous liquors, but the excise duty should have been raised. And for what reason? In order, he says, to prevent the manufacturer from getting rich at the expense of the common people. Always the old grudge! He forgets that protection it is that has made our country what it is to-day; that to it we owe the growth of our cities; that it has saved Canada from the soup-kitchens of the Mackenzie Administration; that it has built and fostered in the large cities, in all the provinces, hives of industry where the workingmen earn a decent living for their wives and children. Protection has made Canada a magnificent country, the pride of its sons and of the empire.
But, Mr. Speaker, to hear the critics of the Opposition, the preferential tariff should not have been raised. This increase is to the prejudice of the Empire. The Empire! This word excites our hon. friends' enthusiasm to its highest pitch. Ask $200,000,000 for the war, they exclaim in unison, and we will vote it; buit do not in anyway increase the tariff against British goods. What folly is yours? Is it not enough that Great Britain should have to fight the submarines which seek to destroy its commerce, without forcing her to pass her goods into Canada over a tariff wall.
This meaningless verbosity and pompousness, Mr. Speaker, might be expected of a tyro in the art of literature but that it should come from the leader of the Opposition is beyond belief. And surely he must know that if the general tariff is increased, the preferential tariff must be increased proportionately, in order to keep between the duty on English-made goods and goods from other countries the same relative difference as existed in the old tariff. But the same policy which prompts the Liberal party to cater to popular prejudices, also induces it to make a loud display of its loyalty to the British Crown. But no one is deceived. The debate on the budget has revived the struggle for power between the two great political parties. As representatives of the people, we are called upon to say which of the two parties is in harmony with the country's aspirations.

Which party built Canada, and has led it to its present state of greatness and pros-pertity? The party of Lafontaine, Macdonald, Cartier, Tupper and Borden. Who brought about this confederation of which we are so proud? The Conservative party. Who inaugurated this system of protection which has made the country great and prosperous? The Conservative party. Who extended the boundaries of this Dominion by the acquisition of the Northwest Territories? Again the Conservative party.
I say that the hon. the leader of the Opposition and his followers have lost the confidence of the electors of Canada and especially those of the province of Quebec; I can speak of that province from closer acquaintance, as I reside therein and the county I have the honour of representing in this House is part and parcel of it. At one time almost the whole of that province was won over to the Liberal party; but the question then at issue appealed to the national and religious sentiment of the electors; it was the famous Manitoba school question. The hon. leader of the Opposition, as he was also then, stood before the electors of Quebec and promised, in return for a strong support from that province, that he, as a French-Canadian and a Catholic, would settle this school question advantageously for the people of Manitoba and to the satisfaction of the population of Quebec. Is it then to be wondered at, Mr. Speaker, that these fiery appeals were successful; that the province pinned its faith in the word of one of its sons, an orator, who, as head of his party, revealed himself a powerful man, invested with all the authority necessary to carry his will into effect. The province confided in him and put him in power. Has he settled that school question in the manner he had pledged himself to do? Assuredly not. He sacrificed the interests of his compatriots and with the object of reaching power, struck a bargain in which the victims were given only scraps of their rights and privileges. Then the present leader of the Opposition ruled this country for many years. All that time the old province of Quebec never lost hope that the pledge given would be redeemed. But nothing was done and one day, in 1911, the hon. leader of the Opposition and his party purposed to hand Canada over to the Americans by means of free-trade with them or reciprocity. What happened? The reply came from the Canadian people, who overthrew the Liberal rule, which my hon. friend is attempting to restore by appealing to popular passion at a

time when the Empire calls for the united energies of all and everyone and when an unswerving loyalty is the imperative duty of the hour, he makes pretence of a deep interest in the needy classes, but this new love bears the stamp of untruthfulness. The utterances of his followers are a tissue of contradictions. We are witnessing a revelry of insane appeals to demagogic prejudices of the populace. Big drums and small drums, flutes and trombone sound a jarring medley. Every one plays as he likes; there. i3 no more any leader; every one speaks for himself, but all aim at the same object, not the triumph of Great Britain over the enemy, although they loudly protest that to be* their goal; but all of them have a common and long cherished aim which was clearly enough expressed by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) when he exclaimed : Let us hope that we shall be rid of this war and this Government at about the same time. But in their hurry these hon. gentlemen would anticipate the issue of the war. Undaunted by the prospect of injuring the British cause by impeding the Government in carrying out its programme of aid and succour, they purpose to overthrow the Government in the very turmoil of the conflict, when all its energies are bent on the execution of its patriotic policy, both national and Imperial. On a mere pretext, for the last four weeks, they have been beleaguering the Administration when a suspension of hostilities had been agreed to and a truce proclaimed. They have played on us the same deception which the Germans practised on the brave Belgians. They suddenly unmasked their batteries and without warning opened fire on the Conservative stronghold. But let them go at it to their heart's content. The Conservative party is strongly entrenched, behind its past achievements and the great expectations justly placed in it; in the love of the Canadian people whose best interests it has always served; in its own determination to see that justice be rendered everyone.
The Rt. Hon. the Prime Minister and his colleagues may well walk with heads erect, for the people of Canada are with them; and in a future that cannot be far distant, the verdict of the people will be voiced in unmistakable fashion by the return to power with an increased majority of the Rt. Hon. Mr. Borden, because he has never failed, since he is at the head of the Government, to consult the best interests of Canada and the Empire.

If
these were ordinary times, and if the Budget which has been presented to (he House by the Finance Minister were an ordinary Budget, I would not take any part in this discussion; but the times are not ordinary and the Budget which the Minister of Finance has submitted to the House, and the speeches with which it has been supported, have been of such an extraordinary character that I do not think I would be doing my duty as a member of this House if I did not say a few words in regard to it.
Unfortunately, I could not follow the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House (Mr. Descarries); consequently I cannot reply to anything he said; I leave that to the hon. gentleman to my right (Mr. Lafortune), who will, I understand, address the House this evening. I have read with some care the speeches of the Finance Minister, and I have come to the conclusion that he is a wonderfully clever and capable man; in fact, he himself has told us so. He has told us that upon his broad shoulders has been placed a burden heavier than that which has been placed upon the shoulders of any other man in his position since Confederation. The responsibilities, the obligations and the liabilities which the hon. gentleman had to assume when he took office would have crushed an ordinary man. But the hon. gentleman did not complain. He tells us that he saw his way clear through from the beginning. He says he saw his way clear through the financial stringency and the hard times of 1912-13; that he saw his way clear through in August last when the outbreak of this terrible war threatened with ruin the finances and the commerce of the whole world; that he sees his way clear through all difficulties to-day, when kingdoms are being shattered and empires are tottering. I am really lost in admiration and wonder. In the words of Cassius, I ask:
In the names of all the gods at once,
Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed
That he has grown so great.
The Finance Minister further tells us that the uncontrolled prodigality, the utter wastefulness and the unbridled' extravagance of the late Government would have ruined this country beyond redemption if they had remained in office a little longer; that he was called in just in the nick of time to save the situation. What a fortunate thing that Canada had such a man at such a time! I do not know how we could

have got along if the Finance Minister had not been discovered. Mr. Speaker, yon have read history, and you know that almost every page, particularly of sacred
10 p.m. history, is replete with instances of how Providence in supreme crises-this is a very consoling thought to us-never failed to raise up great men to lead nations and peoples. The only difference I see 'between those times and the present is that the 'great men of the olden time, so far as I know, never found it necessary or even advisable to announce or proclaim their own greatness. That was probably an oversight on their part; our Finance Minister did not forget that, however.

That may have been the . reason. The hon. minister pointed out to us his capability; his prescience. 'So far from detracting from the hon. gentleman's reputation, I think these words of selfpraise rather add to it, because they show that in the mid-st of his multifarious duties, responsibilities and obligations, he does not forget the smallest detail -which has particular reference to himself.
The hon. gentleman has read political economy, and is a master in finance. In the following words he tells us how to ascertain the solvency of an estate:
In estimating the value of an estate, do we not take into consideration liabilities direct and indirect, debts owing, notes of hand, endorsa-tion, guarantees given by the decedent who left the estate?
Of course we do, hut we take into account also the assets and resources of the estate, hoth direct and indirect. These the hon. gentleman apparently overlooked, because later in his speech he declared in triumphant tones that he himself discharged -all these obligations and liabilities and added hut $8,000,000 to the public debt. At the risk of being arrested, perhaps, for lbse majeste, I venture the assertion that there are one hundred men in Canada-yes, perhaps many more than one hundred-who, under circumstances similar to those in which the hon. minister found himself, would have discharged those obligations and liabilities without adding anything to the public -debt, or who would have reduced the public debt by two or three times $8,000,000. It is my purpose to prove that statement by the public accounts and by the speeches of the hon. gentleman himself.
In looking over the first Budget speech delivered iby my hon. friend, I observe that

it was very different from the -speech which he delivered the other day. I think I should read an extract or two from that speech, which he delivered on March 13, 1912, five months after the present Government resumed office and, of course, five months after the Finance Minister took his present position. He had five months in which to inquire into the solvency of the estate of which he became manager, both in respect of its liabilities and assets; he had five months to inquire into and -make himsel-f familiar with the financial conditions of the country. This is what he said:
The estimated revenue for the current year, with which I am now dealing, being $136,000,000, there will therefore be a surplus of consolidated fund revenue over consolidated fund expenditure of $39,000,000 available for capital and special outlays. I am sure I can congratulate both the House and the country upon what is undoubtedly a record year for the Dominion. I do not know how to quite share that congratulation up, hut as my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) came Into power on the 6th of October, and my right hon friend the leader of the Oppositon was In power prior to that date, there is probably glory enough to go round and it would be the judgment of Solomon that each be entitled to one-half, at all events to a part of the credit for the return which I am now presenting to the House.
That was the situation, that was the financial condition of the country, five months after the hon. gentleman took office. Then he went on to give a statement of the exact figures and said:
Now, Mr. Speaker, what does this mean? It means that out of the abounding revenues of t his country we shall provide for the ordinary current expenditures of the Dominion, for all those large capital outlays which I have mentioned, and which this growing country has required during the year for services of every kind, and at the same time that we shall be able to make a reduction of the public debt to the extent of $1,150,000. "That means, we have more than paid our way, and our surplus has been such that all capital and special charges have been extinguished.
Would you suppose that the Finance Minister would make a speech of that kind, and make this statement, as he did the other day?:
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the late Government were the inventors, the originators, the parents, the progenitors and the propagators of the most inordinate reckless, purblind and wilful extravagance that this country or any other British country has ever known.
I want to read to you an extraet from the Budget speech of the next year to show you the hon. gentleman's opinion of the late Government and of the position of the country at that time. He referred in this speech to the National Transcontinental railway. Before reading his remarks of

May 12, 1913, I should perhaps refer to a short statement made by him in his speech the other day on the same subject:	He
was addressing his remarks directly to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and said:
I say to him now that his railway policy, in its potential consequences, is fraught, and has always -been fraught with the utmost danger to the Dominion of Canada.
I think he referred chiefly to the National Transcontinental railway; but I have always understood that the hon. gentleman who now holds the position of Finance Minister supported that proposition, supported the Government in its railway policy and in its general legislation in all those years, right down to the year 1911, and it therefore seems strange that he should discover all at once that the policy which he had supported ana the party which he had supported for so many years had gone so extremely and outrageously wrong. I do not know when he discovered it and had this change of heart. Inere is a state in Germany called Hesse whose people are callea Hessians. The soldiers from that particular part of the country, for hundreds of years, have fought under every banner and every general in Europe and America. They have fought wherever they could get the best pay. They were ready to enlist under any banner, because they had no convictions and no principles to abandon.
This is what the hon. gentleman stated in regard to railway building on the 12th of May 1913, that is one year and seven months after he became Finance Minister:
The expenditure on the Transcontinental railway reached the considerable sum of over $21,000,000, but as the years of heavy construction have passed the outlays for this service will in the future decline materially.
And a little further on he says:
So far I have dealt with the affairs of the fiscal year 1912-13, and I am sure the results must have been most gratifying to the House, inasmuch as, notwithstanding the generous appropriations which were made for all the services of the country, the net result was practically an equilibrium between the revenue on the one hand and expenditure of all kinds on the other. I am happy to announce that the outcome of the last fiscal year, which ended on March 31, will prove even more satisfactory as reflecting by far the highest pitch to which our national revenues and prosperity have yet attained. The revenue for 1912, as I have stated, amounted to $136,108,217.36. X have every expectation that when the books of the fiscal year 1913 are closed, it will be found that the total revenue will have reached the splendid total of $168,250,000, or an increase over the year 1911-12 of over $32,000,000. Some indication of the magnificent growth of the Dominion may be gleaned from the fact
that this increase in revenue during the period of one year almost equals the entire revenue of the country twenty years ago.
The augmentation of revenue to which I have referred has not been irregular, spasmodic or intermittent in its nature, but has steadily characterized each month of the entire fiscal year. It was, of course, mainly derived from customs receipts, but the other sources of revenue-excise, post office and railways-also gave us very substantial increases.
That was the position of the country and the position of the estate of which the hon. gentleman became manager one year and seven months after he assumed office; and yet we are told, he told us the other afternoon, that the uncontrolled prodigality, the utter wastefulness, the unbridled extravagance of the late Government would have ruined the country beyond redemption if his services had not been obtained. I shall leave that phase of the question for a moment and refer to a sentence that I find in the speech delivered by the hon. gentleman when he submitted his Budget on the 11th of February. It is as follows:
We believe the tariff Increases which we propose will be not only effectual in producing greater revenue but will be strongly efficacious in stimulating Canadian industry and agriculture and in relieving unemployment.
That was the first time in my life that I ever heard that increasing the taxes would produce prosperity. Why the hon. gentleman withheld that remedy far so long I do not know, for he has told us that there were hard times and a financial stringency in 1912-13, and we know that there were hard times and great financial stringency last autumn. The hon. gentleman had this remedy up his sleeve or in his pocket or under his hat all the time, yet Parliament was not called, nor the remedy produced. Perhaps the remedy was withheld until difficulties had accumulated, so that when it was applied it would be all the more striking. I admit that high customs duties may give an artificial stimulus to some industrial concerns, and thus induce people to come off the laud and congregate in the towns and cities; but how that can stimulate agriculture I cannot understand; and I understand the hon. gentleman favours the " back to the land " movement. How he can induce people to settle on the land when he is persuading them to eome into the towns and cities passes my comprehension.
I agree, as far as my knowledge goes, that the increase in the customs duties may and probably will increase the revenue. But if the manufacturing concerns in Canada take full advantage of the increased customs

duties by raising the price of their manufactured articles to that extent, that would not prevent importation, because the importer, generally speaking, would then be relatively in as good a position as he is now. But at what a cost would this increased revenue be obtained! The price of the imported article and the price of the homemade article would be increased to the full extent of the increased customs duty. It is estimated that.four or five times as much is manufactured in Canada as is imported; in some lines the proportion is higher, but generally speaking we manufacture four or five times as much as we import; so that for every dollar raised for the public revenue under those circumstances at least four or five dollars would have to be paid by the people, and would find its way into the pockets of somebody at the expense of the consumers of the country. Again, let us suppose that the manufacturers do not take full advantage of the increased customs duties, and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) told us the other night that the concern with which he is connected would not raise the prices of their manufactured articles. In that case, the importations will be greatly reduced, and the Finance Minister may not get the revenue he expects. Suppose the manufacturers take advantage of the increased customs duties to two-thirds or three-quarters of the increase, the revenue would then be increased, but there would be the disadvantage of the increased price upon all imports and upon all manufactured articles in Canada; and the consumer would lose probably three or four times what the revenue had gained. But that is not the worst feature of it, according to my way of thinking. The worst feature is that the Government is in a large measure placing in the hands of a body .of irresponsible citizens-I care not how respectable they may be-whose personal interests are directly opposed to the public interests, the power to say what the revenues of the country shall be. In other words, they are farming out the collection of the taxes. Some years ago I read in some book that that was the system that prevailed in Turkey, and in Egypt before the British occupation. The tax collectors,
I forget their technical name, were sent into the outlying districts and provinces and allowed to collect as much as they could, provided they remitted a certain portion to Constantinople, the headquarters, to be spent on luxuries there. We sympathize with the 
people who had to submit to that kind of government; but is our system of raising the revenue vastly different from that of the Turks? When we are in a large measure handing over one of the vital functions of government to an irresponsible body of citizens, can we be so sure that we obtained responsible government in this country some seventy or eighty years ago?
I wish to quote again a statement made by the Minister of Finance, because it is worth repeating, and to refer him to the public accounts which were prepared by him or by the Government of which he is a member. In his speech the other night he said:
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the late Government were the inventors, the originators, the parents, progenitors and propagators of the most inordinate, reckless, purblind and wilful extravagance that this country or any other British country has ever known.
That is certainly a most astonishing statement to make; and if the late Government were guilty of all that extravagance I would ask my hon. friend to supply me with language to describe the extravagance of this Government for certainly I could not do it justice. I invite the hon. gentleman's attention to a few of the items in public accounts. Take civil government, for instance. That is a branch of the Government service in which there should be very little increase from year to year, for it comprises the salaries and contingencies of the offices at Ottawa and of the High Commissioner's office in London, and the salaries of the lieutenant governors. It is, therefore, a branch of the public service in which there should not be much increase from year to year, and I find that for 15 years under the late Administration there was very little change, the average yearly increase from 1896 to 1911 having been in round figures $200,000. The average yearly increase for the three years of this Government was upwards of $380,000, nearly twice as much as the yearly increase under the late Government. As far as I can understand these things, there is no justification for that at all; can the Minister of Finance suggest any defence?
I will take some of the other accounts just in the order in which they come, though not in the order of their merit. I find that from 1896 to 1911, under the Liberal Government, the average yearly increase in the expenditure chargeable to Consolidated Revenue Fund was $3,400,000, and under this Government it has been $13,200,000, or $9,800,000 per annum greater than during

the Liberal regime, or 290 per cent greater.
I would be pleased if the Minister of Finance would tell us how to describe that. The Prime Minister himself declared that the late Government was extravagant beyond all possible defence. In the expenditure chargeable on Consolidated Fund Account, you will find the yearly increase under the Liberal Administration to be $3,400,000, and under this Government to be $13,200,000. If this Government had been satisfied with the yearly increase made by its predecessor, it would have saved in round figures $10,000,000 per year.
I do not know what defence can be offered for such extravagance. The hon. gentleman is trying to be facetious. I have proved-

I have proved the correctness of the statement made by the Toronto Globe a short time ago, that this Government was spending money like a drunken sailor. That statement is below the mark. If this unbridled extravagance has been maintained under this 'Government in time of peace, we may well ask what has been done in time of war. We know already a little of what has been done-we know that small druggists and drug clerks dn the city of Ottawa-in -a night-in the twinkling of an eye-have blossomed into wholesale druggists, 'and have obtained orders from the Government ranging from fifteen to forty thousand dollars, on which profits of 40 per cent to 80 peT cent have been made. We know that dozens of automobiles have been bought at very high prices, and that many of them have disappeared as completely as if the ground had opened and swallowed them. We know that sets of motor tires have been purchased for more than six hundred dollars a set, the wholesale price of which is less than three hundred. We know that members of Parliament and others, who would not know a hackney from a clydesdale, were commissioned to buy horses for the army; that many of the horses so bought were found to be unfit for duty and had to be 'Sold for what they would bring, and that many of them disappeared altogether.
Mr. A. De WITT FOSTER: Will the hon.
member offer to the House some proof of that statement ? If he refers to any act in which I have participated, I have already placed my denial on the pages of Hansard, and it is quite unfair for the hon. gentleman to make a statement without producing the proof.

We know that a young lady typist in the office of the Minister of Militia and Defence patented a shovel; and that as soon as the minister examined it he found it to be so useful for trench-digging and other purposes that he immediately ordered 25,000 of them-and he is still ordering more shovels. We know that the war grafters have hung like a cloud of locusts around the Government, and around the
troops; and that while spouting loyalty with their lips they have taken their blood-toll wherever they can find it. We know that the brave men who have offered their lives for their country have been given equipment that has cost enormous prices, but is entirely unfit for service. We know that they were supplied with boots that soaked in water like a sponge; and that if it had not been for the intervention of the home Government they would have been sent into the trenches in France and Belgium maimed and crippled for life before they saw the enemy. We know that the Auditor General tried to save the people of Canada from being robbed to the extent of hundreds of thousands of dollars; but we have not discovered where he got any assistance from the Government or from any member of the Government. We know that many of these practices are still going on, and that the Government is not ignorant thereof; but ignorance in such a case would be no excuse-it would be nearly as culpable as actual participation in the guilt.
The Government as a whole is responsible, and every member of the Government must take his share of the responsibility for these things. The Treasury Board must take its share. The Finance Minister must take his full share. But there is one man who above all the others must bear the odium of the guilt and the disgrace, and, as Nathan said unto David, so I say unto the Prime Minister, " Thou art the man."

Mr. Speaker, as I rise
to take part in this debate, my first utterances have special reference to the hon. ithe Minister of Finance (Mr. White), who enjoyed the most unusual privilege of being called to the cabinet in preference to certain friends of his, men of weight and ability, men with a wider range of experience, better informed, and having to their credit many years of parliamentary life; men well up in years who had long waited, no doubt, for recognition by their leader. But the hon. minister had qualities which placed him above all those gentlemen: he was a Liberal and all his life had been at the school of the distinguished followers of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. So early recognition was to be his, and it is no surprise that he should have taken precedence over his colleagues. He belongs to the privileged class, which explains the liberties he allows himself when referring to his erstwhile friends. I may say to him: it is your right, but you are

wanting in gratitude for -the party with which you had always been connected, the pafty in which you have received youi political education.
It was a pleasure to listen to the speech of the new member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Descarries), a man of parts, a distinguished member of the Montreal bar and with whom I have the honour of being well acquainted. He is one of my good friends, and also, I beg to tell him, the representative of the electoral division in which I reside. Therefore I owe him all the respect and consideration due from an elector to the member for his county.
His opening remarks were just and most appropriate. He alluded to the late Mr. Monk, ex-Minister of Public Works, in tones both solemn and grave. It was fit and proper and with the same feelings I wish to pay honour to the memory of the distinguished citizen who, before my hon. friend, was the representative of my county. -But the hon. gentleman has sinned against the canons of history in curtailing the truth. He stated that the late Mr. Monk was a distinguished man: I agree; quite so. A man of uncommon worth: But he has forgotten to state the reasons for his retiring from the Government. The hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier who has just entered Parliament, loses sight of certain particulars. He was not here when the ex-Minister of Public Works twitted on the dissensions in the ranks of his party and among the ministers, replied from his seat in the House:	" Do not fret! I am
riveted, bolted, padlocked to my seat." Yes, hut his rivets had no heads, his locks no keys and his bolts no nuts. The next day he made his last bow to his colleagues and departed.
The intimate confidences of the ex-Minister of Public Works show that he was disgusted with his friends and their policies.
Mr. Monk was a man of talent, intelligent and honourable, true to his public statements and faithful to the pledges he had made to the electorate. Have his (friends followed his example? This the hon. member for Jacques Cartier failed to disclose. Yet this is an important point. One thing however is certain, he the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, has not followed in the footsteps of the late minister.
My hon. 'friend speaks of patriotism. Patriotism is a noble sentiment. The word fits well in a speech of the 24th of June. On that day we loudly proclaim our respect for our clergy, our schools, our institutions and our language. This on ,the -24th of 
June. But, Mr. Speaker, their cheers of the 25th are: Hurrah for Borden! Hurrah for his policy! But 1 say every day of the year. Hurrah for Laurier! Hurrah for his policy! And by these I stand publicly on the 24th of June as staunchly as on the next day.
Can the hon member recall what he stated during the campaign of 19X1? These gentlemen, nationalists of all grades, have in the meantime forgotten many things. At that time the hon. member was heard to cry out: Electors of Jacques Cartier, let us have no navy! Down with the navy! No contribution to imperial defence without consulting the people. These clamours have now escaped his memory. How times have changed! One day must not be held accountable for another. Once on a time there was a certain man, a demagogue, who had succeeded in throwing into confusion public opinion by shouting:	Down with
the Laurier navy! and no Borden contribution to imperial defence previous to consulting the people. And all this the hon. member has forgotten. Of the leader whom to-day he rightly regards with respect and whose eulogy he makes, he then said: Down with Borden! We shun Laurier's policy but we abhor Borden's which is worse. Is it not strange, Mr. Speaker, that tve should hear nothing of this? A singular deficiency of memory, indeed.
It cannot be proven that I have ever uttered such words.

What! But all this is ancient history. I expected your denial, because all those who attacked the Canadian navy have afterwards repudiated their utterances as you have just done. We have never been Nationalists, they asserted. When the hon. member for Champlain was asked if he was a Nationalist, he denied it and he was appointed Deputy Speaker.

I
would like to ask the hon. member if he has ever been a Conservative?
As you have been a Liberal.

The
opportunity is now given me to remind him that he has not always been a good Tory. Why open a discussion on this subject when the hon. member once fought against

his old leader, Mr. Mousseau, shielded behind Mr. Laflamme.

What
change time works in a man! The hon. member for Jacques Cartier is well known. He has furnished the subject of a pamphlet, a poem, where he is represented as a poli

 tical chameleon. I should have been silent on this subject; but the hon. member is playing with fire when he states that I have once been a Tory. He asserts what is not true and knowingly. But Judases there are in every land, as there was one even in Holy Land. Everywhere there are deserters. Here some men retire in the evening Liberals and wake up in the morning Conservatives. the integrity and the prosperity of our country. about the Transcontinental?

The

At the sight of the men who supported Mr. Bourassa, the question suggests itself to me:	Where do they stand to-day?

She
applauded him because he is an eloquent man, a talented man high above any of you.
His policy was that not a cent should be given without an appeal to the people.
Meanwhile his stand has been a consistent one and reliance may be placed in his word.
To-day these genltlemen wave the British flag. It is their business, but I prefer the man who keeps his word. The cry was spread that the Canadians were about to be sent to foreign lands to be cut to pieces by shot and shell. The triumph of the Conservative party was brought about by seditious appeals to the people. Bourassa took the lead and had it not been for his eloquence, many who are sitting in this House to-day would have been left at home. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mir. Sevigny), who is to-day deputy speaker of the House of Commons, a distinguished gentleman, a talented orator, declared before the electors, with tears in his voice, that he was opposed to the navy. And according to the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Rainville), who belongs to an old Liberal family, the Liberals were not worth a great deal; he alone deserved the confidence of the people. There have been traitors in our ranks. Judas is of all times and all countries. Some we know who, Liberals when they retire in the evening went forth in the morning Conservatives. They bring to my mind the five turncoats of Quebec. In the evening they voted confidence in Mr. Joly and next morning their votes went for Mr. Chapleau. They all had their reward. One received a judgeship another was called to the cabinet: each one received his price.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier spoke of his friends sincerely and of the legacies left by the Liberals when they gave up the reins of power. But what harvest did the Liberals reap in 1896 from the Conservatives' sowing? We at least have no Curran bridge, no McGreevy affair, no Pacific scandal, and none of those other scandals too numerous to enumerate, but which the whole country has witnessed.
Hon. gentlemen opposite thought they had at least unearthed in the Transcontinental railway a burrow of graft and maladministration, but since the report has

been tabled, nothing more has been said about it. The Transcontinental railway is a national enterprise and Laurier was the only man able to cope with this gigantic task.
The Pacific scandal has crushed the Conservative party under public odium. The party's chieftain, Sir John A. Macdonald, a statesman, was heard to exclaim: " These hands are clean "; but others were not able to say as much. Yes, many hands indeed were found to be unclean when the McGreevy-Connelly scandal was ventilated.

This admonition bears witness to the excellence of the Liberal Administration; it is a certificate of efficiency.

Oh ! Oh!
