dissolute. I was there. He charged Mr. Prevost with having returned from Belgium with young lady secretaries. Is that not the same thing? and the way it was said, there was no mistaking the meaning. It was clear French to us.
All these gentlemen, Mr. Speaker, will before long have to render an account of their actions to the electors. Let them not think that the public will forget. The people may be deceived in a moment ot passion; their good faith may be ensnared once, nut not twice. The hon. member spoke of his leader's respectability and the harmony that reigns in his party. The harmony was nothing to boast of when Sir Mackenzie Bowell stated from his seat in the House that among those who surrounded him was a nest of

traitors, serpents and reptiles. The hon. member was silent on this point. He has forgotten the history of his party. He should refreshen his memory. Never has the Liberal party given the spectacle of similar scandals. It has always been free from serpents and reptiles.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has claimed for his party the honour of having made Canada the great country it is to-day. In 1878, when Alexander Mackenzie went out of power, the Conservative party inaugurated the National Policy. From 1878 to 1896, the country was in dire distress. The people were poor; industry was languishing; factory hands had one or two days' work a week; the French-Canadians in sheer discouragement were migrating to the United States; farms were being sold and the parishes abandoned. Desolation spread over the land. With the National Policy the great West remained undeveloped.
In 1896, Sir Wilfrid Laurier came to power and with the same tariff, the same Laurier, who is now the butt of your criticisms, transformed the country. We are not against protection in itself, so long as it is sensibly applied. Manufacturers, representative people in every walk of life, came or sent delegations to the Government asking that protection be not abolished. Sir Wilfrid Laurier reduced it 17)- per cent. Now, Mr. Speaker, how comes it that the hon. gentlemen on your right with the same tariff, and in the same country, obtained results the very opposite of ours which had culminated in a great and prosperous Canada. Where is the explanation? Is it not proof that they had not managed the country's affairs as prudent men of business should do? The hon. member for Jacques Cartier recalled the great names of Lafontaine, Cartier, Macdonald, Tupper and Borden. That they were distinguished statesmen is admitted by every one; but I must make an exception as to the last named politician. So far as he is concerned I abide by the testimony-of his Nationalist friends.
I am not one of those who pretend that the Conservative party has done nothing for the country. I concede that great national undertakings have been carried out by the Conservatives; but for all that, it ill fits the member for Jacques Cartier to say that the Liberals are demagogues.
I expected better from his first speech. He went on the wrong track. Another time he may be more careful.
The hon. member has brought forward the question of the Manitoba schools. But

what will you do regarding the question of the schools in Ontario? At the present time collections are made in the churches of the province of Quebec to help ithe causa.

Will my
hon. friend state whether he thinks that under the British North America Act, the Government can do something in this respect?

Why,
then, did the hon. member refer to it in his speech last Friday?

My answer is I believe that personally we can do something; but does my hon. friend hold that under the British North America Act, we can interfere, when the Ontario minority is not appealing to the Governor General in Council?
This is something new. These gentlemen spoke differently when.the Manitoba school question was at issue.

I ask my
hon. friend to keep to the question he has raised regarding the rights of the Ontario minority.

I ask
my hon. friend to seek his information from the member for Jacques Cartier or the member for Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche). The latter is a distinguished lawyer, who knows more law than the doctor. The member for Nicolet has not taken the same position on this question that the hon. member for IAlslet has taken. I prefer the opinion of the member for Nicolet to that of the member for L'Islet as to the interpretation of the British North America Act. The learned doctor knows more about maple sugar and maple syrup than about the British North America Act. Let each one confine himself to his trade, let each one follow his profession; a cobbler must not set himself to shoeing horses.

The hon.
member might reply, not to Doctor Paquei of Saint Aubert, in the county of L'lslet, but to the member for L'Islet.

They
are of the same family and let them wrangle with each other.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has attempted to show the deep affection of the Canadian people for the Conservative party. This affection has come rather late. Have (the people been so very fond of the Conservative party since 1896? This party
came out of the elections of 1900 and 1904 crushed under an overwhelming defeat. In 1902, it was again beaten at the polls. The affection of which my hon. friend boasts came in 1911, and was born of falsehood and deceit. It is like a step-mother's love, of short duration.
The hon. gentlemen say that in 1911 their triumph came unexpectedly. Success came to them as a surprise, because their cause was bad. But there is strength behind an unchallenged lie. Bourassa had rushed all over the province stirring the people over the terrible consequences of war; nobody answered him; the Liberals let him alone. A man of Bourassa's ability, a powerful orator, fills the province with his eloquence and no one replies to him. Is it to be wondered at, Mr. Speaker, that people have put faith in his statements? Everywhere Bourassa boasted that Laurier and his friends did not dare take the platform and contradict him. And the people would naturally say: Bourassa is right, otherwise the Liberals would take the trouble of refuting him. But, Mr. Speaker, when he came into my county, your humble servant whose knowledge is limited, who is no match for him, at least courageous enough to meet him and forbid him to speak in his county unless he himself spoke on the same platforms; and D. A. spoke against him fearlessly. D. A. did not hide as many did. D. A. stood up and still stands, and I invite him at the next election to come in my county if I am again a candidate. I am not a man of great parts. I have no pretensions to science or eloquence but in justice I must be credited with a good deal of spirit.
When the Keewatin school question was before the House-and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier who alluded to the Manitoba school question should not have forgotten this point-did the Conservatives proceed to settle it as they had promised to do? They had the authority; why did they not exercise iit? Did not Bishop Charlebois ask the Government to settle the question? The Government did not make a move. The schools of Keewatin were sacrificed. I heard some priests applying to the Government the epithet " sans-coeur "; the fathers of Saint Lawrence told me that these gentlemen had deceived them odiously.
The question is akin to that of the French language in the schools of Ontario. The attempt is made to deprive the French-Canadians of their language in the schools, as if under the Treaty o'f Paris, at the time of the cession of Canada to England, the use of our language had not been

I rise to a point of order, I hope the hon. member will understand that it is not to the credit either of the House or himself to introduce Lady Laurier's name in the debate. For the sake of decorum in this House, I ask the hon. member to have enough dignity and decency to refrain from that sort of talk.

Hear
the member for Vercheres speak of dignity!
I was saying that when the colleagues of the learned member were attempting to prevent the leader of the Opposition from speaking after you, Mr. Speaker, had given him the floor, Lady Laurier wept at the sight of the treatment meted out to her husband.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think is is hardly
compatible with the dignity of the House to refer to those who occupy seats in the gallery during the sittings of the House.

I submit to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and I shall leave this subject aside.
When I saw that the leader of the Opposition was prevented from speaking, I could not but think that it was a most regrettable and most painful proceeding; yet the hon. member applauded long with his friends. Such action was without excuse and I say that those guilty of it will pay back a hundredfold the insult and outrage offered to the leader of a great party. There may be some difference of opinion between us but we should be fair to one another, and since the Speaker had found it fair and reasonable to grant the floor to the leader of the Opposition, his right to speak should not have been taken away from him by a mere majority vote. Such things should not

happen and such a course cannot be tolerated indefinitely and without amends being made.

Eight
per cent.

Nine
per cent.
Oh! I can outbid you; I say ten per cent.

As I
have still much to say and many questions to deal with, which may require some little time, I will, with the consent of the hon. minister move the adjournment of the debate.

I understand that the
whips have come to an arrangement by which two other hon. gentlemen are to speak to-night. I hope, therefore, that the hon. gentleman will be able to finish his speech.

I am ready to go on, but you will have to be patient. It will take me more than an hour to finish.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I represent a county essentially agricultural, and the remarks I am about to make are in the best interests of that county and of the farming community in general. I think that when a member is elected, he is no longer Liberal or Conservative, but he is the representative of the whole county and must look after the interests of every one. It is the same thing with ministers of the Crown. In a county represented by a Liberal member there are not Liberals only, but there is a mixed population to such an extent sometimes that the majority is very small and there are no longer Liberals and Conservatives, but solely electors.
I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Finance very particularly to the tobacco industry which in recent years has made great progress. Years ago our annual production of tobacco was only one or two millions of pounds. Now it is eleven millions of pounds and that the producers may succeed, we must give them a share of protection. I grow tobacco myself. 1 planted ten acres last year and I gathered . in ten thousand pounds which are being prepared for the market. It is not generally known how expensive this crop is. With the present tariff as it stands, there is no big money to be made. Only the farmer who gets up at five o'clock iii the morning and works until sunset, along with his wife and children, can succeed in'"'making a
profit that is worth while; but not all farmers can or will do that. An increase was and is asked of the duty on foreign tobaccos. The manufacturers, of course, object to an increase because the easier the conditions under which they can import foreign tobacco, the less Canadian tobacco will they need.. If this duty which we ask was imposed, the manufacturers would have to purchase Canadian tobacco in order to mix it with the imported leaf; and the Canadian producer would be benefited thereby.
I submit these remarks to the consideration of the hon. Minister of Finance and hope that he will grant the request of the farmers.
I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not here, because my remarks are especially on an agricultural topic. I would like to see in the estimates a grant to help the farmers in building curing sheds. The growing of tobacco cannot be a success without them; and the same thing should be done by the Government for curing sheds as was done for butter and cheese factories.
Where does the hon. member want them built?
I would grant a bonus to every tobacco grower who built one on his farm. This would permit him to get better equipment and to produce a better tobacco.

If the constituents of the hon. gentleman requested that the Hon. Mr. Caron, Minister of Agriculture for the province of Quebec, should apply for a grant for the purpose, to be appropriated from the Dominion vote, I think the hon. member would get it.
I am in a position to state to the hon. member for Chambly that the thing that he suggests has been done; but the Dominion grant is not sufficient. Mr. Caron has no money to help the farmers.

It would certainly be possible to lay aside $50,000 for this purpose.
Mr. iLAFORTUNE (Translation): This is what I ask.

You
could certainly get it out of the Dominion grant.

No. 1 found this out for myself. The Dominion grant is certainly insufficient to allow the



Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec to consider my request. If a grant equal to one-half the cost should be allowed to every farmer who builds a first-class curing house, it would greatly further the tobacco growing industry. The dairy industry was fostered in many ways; the farmer was induced to discard old-fashioned methods and to build up-to-date butter and cheese factories. He was granted substantial help. Why should not the same thing be done the tobacco industry? I represent an essentially agricultural community, a beautiful and extensive country, and if I am still its representative in the next Parliament, I shall have to travel one hundred miles to visit it fully. This is enough to show that at the present moment, I am fulfilling an important duty. Montcalm country lies north of the Laurentian mountains. Within its bounds are to be found sixty lakes abounding with fish; there are forests which have never echoed the woodman's axe, actually within forests; there is a wide surface of splendid arable land and it .is one of the largest constituencies in the province. The production of tobacco is the chief industry of Montcalm county and should ever the hon. Minister of Finance wish to smoke a good pipe of tobacco, let him try the tobacco raised in my county or in Essex county. Our tobacco is favourably known, but if the farmers of the counties of L'Assomption, Berthier, Joliette, and especially Terrebonne are to succeed they must be given protection by means of an increased duty on the foreign article.
There is already a duty of 28 cents per pound on these foreign tobaccos, but this is not sufficient.
The minister has had the courtesy to receive a large joint deputation of tobacco growers from Quebec and Ontario. The delegates were tendered a cordial reception by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Inland Revenue. Splendid speeches were made and all possible encouragement was promised. The numerous delegates asked the ministers to impose an increased duty of seven cents on imported tobacco. This request is altogether legitimate. Last year
22,000,000 pounds of tobacco passed the Canadian Customs. Now, if an additional tax of seven cents a pound were imposed, it would mean a big reduction in these importations, which mean a ruinous competition to the Canadian weed.
The American tariff imposes a duty of V0 cents a pound on foreign tobaccos. It is a prohibitive duty. The markets of the United States are practically closed to our tobacco. Why then should we allow into

the country foreign tobaccos to the extent of 22,000,000 pounds? Such would not be the case if our request for an increase of seven cents in the duty were granted I do hope that, after receiving serious consideration, it will be granted. So far as I an; concerned, I hope our farmers will continue to improve their methods of cultivation so as to place on the market a product still better than what we have to-day. The minister who witnessed how earnest the delegates were in asking this protection against foreign competition, must have been convinced of the necessity of this measure. Besides the increase of seven cents in the duty, the delegates further asked the Government that means be taken to abolish trusts and combines which are so harmful to the grower. Some manufacturers get together and fix themselves the price they wish to pay. The farmer has no control, the combine is the judge and master. These trusts are powerful and the growers cannot keep up the fight they are putting up against them. They actually control the price of tobacco. Why do you see the dairy industry take so much importance? It is due to the encouragement it receives. Why not do the same for tobacco? The counties of Montcalm and Joliette afford particular facilities for the tobacco-growing industry. If the farmers had the means of getting all the necessary equipment they could market a better product. They should receive a grant to help them in building curing sheds. Let the Government make them the necessary advances on reasonable terms of repayment.
Another question to which I wish to draw the attention of the Government is that of tobacco seed. It should be supplied to the farmer. Those who know will acknowledge that it is perhaps the most important point. Good seed is essential to the production of tobacco of the best kind. At the present time, the grower goes to the store, asks for Comstock Spanish seed and is given Kentucky seed. Such errors often happen to the loss of the grower. He expects a certain kind of tobacco and gets an entirely different kind. I discussed the matter with the Superintendent of the Tobacco Branch of the Experimental Farm and he agrees with me. The tobacco seed should be supplied. The expense would be slight, but the question becomes important when so many errors are made by merchants who in perfect good faith because they themselves have been deceived, sell bad seed or seed of one variety when another variety is required. That has happened about fifty times at Saint Jacques,

Saint Alexis, Saint Esprit, and elsewhere. I maintain that the Superintendent of the Tobacco Branch at Ottawa should have enough seed to distribute to farmers, so as to prevent such mistakes. I am aware, of course, that if I ask this official for tobacco seed he will give it to me in exchange for the price, but I say it should be given free of charge. I can pay for it, but I claim it should be given to the farmers.
Another question which deserves the attention of the Minister of Agriculture is the drainage of farms in Ontario and Quebec. In those provinces, substantial grants were at first made for that purpose, but were afterwards discontinued; why, I do not know. When the Government put that policy into effect, general satisfaction was expressed. Farmers congratulated themselves, thinking that stones lying about would be removed, and that the embankments of ditches would be levelled down and the water given free access to the ditches. But that did not last. Was there friction of some kind between the Dominion and Provincial Governments? I do not know. I spent $1,500 of my own money to drain my land, hut not everybody can do that. Grain, potatoes, and corn cannot grow in water. Intensive cultivation cannot succeed in undrained land. Fruit trees also require a good drainage. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier understands drainage. He knows what beautiful orchards surround Montreal. The success of the orchards at Cote des Neiges, Notre-Dame de Grace, Coteau St. Pierre, Dorval and elsewhere was due to the land being naturally drained, while the failure at Pointe Claire, Saint Anne, Saint Laurent, lie Bizard, was due to the unfavourable conditions offered by a water-logged soil. Apple trees, plum trees and cherry trees will not thrive in undrained land unless planted on hillsides. I claim that drainage should be given the same encouragement that was given to the cheese and butter industries and to the postal service, etc. The farming community must get more consideration than it has had in the past at the hands of the Government. I called on the Hon. Mr. Caron, Minister of Agriculture for the province of Quebec, a pains-taking minister- and apparently a practical agriculturist, and he acknowledged as I do the necessity of draining the farms.
Yes, but a minister who is rather parsimonious.

Rather, but one could not expect him to give what he had not. The farmers do not possess the o6i
means of draining their lands when they are flooded. The situation is not the same as is to be found at Varennes on the old homesteads. That is the finest parish in the province. But elsewhere the ease is different. Around Montreal, the land, for lack of drainage, does not even afford good grazing, because they have not the necessary ditches to drain off the surplus water. A quarter and sometimes one-half the land is not drained. All the newspapers report the earnest intention on the part of the Dominion Government to encourage the development of agriculture and secure larger returns. That is a commendable policy. The farmers must be given the means of success. Now, I claim that the Dominion Government should help the provincial authorities by granting them a fair amount to be distributed so as to secure those improvements which will render agriculture more profitable and the farmer more prosperous. It is useless to speak of progress in agricultural pursuits if the basis of them all, that is the land, is not first given proper attention. This is elementary. Begin first by draining the land, for heavy rains cause the cereals to rot and may in quick order destroy the results of your efforts. The farmers therefore should be encouraged to drain their land by giving them a grant equal to one-half the expenditure. This grant would be given only where the work has been done according to approved methods and on an inspector's certificate that it has been done in accordance with the requirements and in a proper way.
Macdonald College could furnish the necessary information.

Yes,
but it is a private institution and I fear they would not furnish it. I have asked the Department of Agriculture at Quebec to send engineers to show me where the ditches should be dug out. They sent me an engineer from the Macdonald Farm who made the plans and instructed me how to carry them out.
The information given out by the Ottawa Experimental Farm should be more widely distributed; and for this purpose agricultural stations should be established. Hon. Mr. Fisher, Minister of Agriculture in the Laurier Government, had agreed to consider the proposal and to attempt the establishment of such stations.
But he lacked the time to do it. He was satisfied with giving pledges.
Farmers form a most important part of the community, and they need protection on account of their restricted means.
You are now converted to protection.

I never was opposed to protection intelligently applied. I am a good party man, as every one knows, but not such as to follow blindly. I look at this question, as at all others, from the viewpoint of the practical man. A stock of pamphlets, circulars and seed grain should be left in those agricultural stations for the benefit of the farmers. This scheme is of interest to all the farmers in the land and should have the support of my hon. friends opposite. I have failed as yet to persuade the minister, but I do not despair that before long every one will acknowledge as I do the necessity of establishing these branches of the Experimental Farm. I have no desire to depreciate the work done by that national institution, which gives excellent results and is absolutely necessary to the development of our agriculture, but I do say that with its present system of organization, it does not achieve the purpose for which it was established. I once accompanied a party of two hundred farmers who visited the farm. We saw splendid exhibits and magnificent stock: horses, cattle, sheep, hogs. But one has only time to glance at this, while he would like to stop and examine, and get a fund of information. As things are at present, it is impossible, through lack of time, to obtain the information one would wish. Our farmers are anxious to learn; they are ready to go far in the way of expenditure, provided they be given some help. This particular class of the population, it is worth repeating, deserves special protection. It is not the lawyer, doctor or notary who builds up the country, but the man behind the plough. The fact is acknowledged in all countries. The tilling of the soil is the noblest of occupations. The farmers in Canada are seventy per cent of the population, and they are afforded the least protection of all classes. Now, I claim for them no privileges, but elementary justice. Who built the schools, the churches, the presbyteries; who built everything in this country, if not the agriculturist? So it is not charity that I beg for him; it is equal justice that I demand. How was the country peopled? It is not to city inhabitants that the larger number of children are born, but to country people. While only a few little ones are to be found

in the home of the manufacturer or the professional man, the farmer's cottage shelters ten, twelve and even fifteen children. Agriculture is the source of all progress. It is the nurse of the State. But what protection does she get, when duties are imposed on agricultural implements, threshing machines, ploughs, harrows, rakes, harvesters, rollers, etc.? Such is the protection afforded. Does the legislator act wisely in putting duty on farming implements? Why not rather raise the duty on silk goods, laces and velvets? Why not increase the tax on whiskey, tobacco and all things superfluous? I state the imposts on farm appliances are a national crime.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I beg to call to the hon. member's attention the fact that there is an understanding between the two parties, and that two other orators are to follow him. It might be well if he would cut his remarks as short as possible.

I am
sorry, but I feel I would not be doing my duty if I failed to say all I have to say. It will take me about half an hour longer. I say to the Hon. Minister of Finance: Take off the taxes now weighing upon agricultural implements. Impose your taxes on silks, velvets and beautiful flowers.

The
duties on these are high enough already.

Raise
them again. If a lady wants tq wear a $50 hat, let her pay for it.
There is something else I should like to see modified. Under the late Administration, fry was distributed to all those who wished to restock the lakes and rivers. That practice has been stopped. There are sixty lakes in my county, and fish is getting scantier on account of the large number of tourists. Some years ago the fry was given 'free and placed in the lakes by Government employees. To-day we cannot get it, I myself own a lake in the North. To-day the fry must be bought. Will the Government derive a great benefit from this sale? Of course not. Why not distribute the fry free of charge so as to continue to stock 'our lakes?
The poultry industry should also receive Government help. It is to be regretted that in Canada this industry is so little encouraged. Financial aid should be granted the farmers to help them in building model poultry yards. At such times as these when the supply of eggs is not sufficient to meet the demands of the market, I say it

is time that our farmers be helped to take the hens out of the cow-house into first-class poultry yards, where they would lay more eggs. If the egg market is not supplied as it should be, what is the reason? It is due to the negligence of our farmers and their lack of means to build a proper hen-house.
It does not cost very much, and the Dominion Government allows the provincial government a grant of $25,000 which could be utilized for the purpose.

I do
not know how that money is spent. If a farmer wishes to lay out a model poultry yard, he writes the department at Quebec, who sends two carpenters. They build the hen-roost. It is something, but more is required. The Dominion Government ought to determine the amount to be spent on each poultry-house, so that sufficient eggs may be marketed to supply the demand. I had some hens and built a model poultry-house that cost nie perhaps a little more than it should, hut it was for my own satisfaction. That industry must be encouraged by all possible means. The Government should make it known to the farmers that if they build poultry-houses according to certain definite rules as to plan and material, one-half the cost would after construction be paid by the Government. The barn would no more serve as a hen-roost. This experiment is worth attempting. Millions of dollars have been given to the railways; why should not some encouragement of the kind I have mentioned be extended to the farmers. Railways have been built, roads have been opened, courthouses, registry offices, penitentiaries have been erected. Why should not the farmer receive the help I have suggested? This class of the population deserves to be especially protected.
There is	another measure which	mustbe	carried	out,	Mr. Speaker. The cryis	general	that	children must be	sentto	school,	and	that the exodus	from
the rural districts into the cities must be stopped. This is an excellent policy, but in order that the child be kept on the soil, he must be taught agriculture. Why is there not a school-garden annexed to every school? Why not have on the school grounds a kitchen-garden by which to instil into the pupils the love of agriculture, as is done in Europe, as was done especially in that unfortunate country, Belgium, which has just been overthrown?
She has not been overthrown.

j Not utterly overthrown; but she can come to her own again only with the help that will be given her; but that she does is my earnest wish.
The Minister of Agriculture, in my opinion, should set aside in his estimates a certain sum to establish school-gardens, and appoint an inspector, a practical man, whose duty it would be to prepare pupils, not perhaps on, the same scale as at Grignon College, in France, but at any rate to give them practical lessons. A real benefit would accrue therefrom to the farming community, and there would not be so many young girls dreaming of nothing but dress, theatres, and moving pictures. How can a child have a liking for agriculture when he is ignorant of its very elementary principles? In this elementary experiments in the school-garden, the pupil will be doing on a small scale what later he will be called on to do in the larger field of the farm.
A word also on apiculture. It should be taught at school. But in this country bee-keeping is only an infant industry. No farm is complete without hives. While at Chateauguay last year I visited the apiary of a Mr. Beaudin. This gentleman had an humble beginning, but success attended his efforts and to-day he is reputed a rich man.
On reading the statistics of old European countries, we find that the yield of hay is at its best only where bees are kept. The -same holds good for the orchards. Yet no encouragement is offered here to the keeping of bees. My suggestion is that a certain grant -should be made to every farmer who constructs an apiary.
Another question which in my humble opinion is not without importance is the lack of encouragement given to ploughing competitions. It gives me pleasure to see at his seat the new member for Jacques Cartier. He will listen to me as he is wont to do, respectfully. I would ask him to stir up his friends to help towards establishing an annual fair at Montreal. The Montreal members seem quite indifferent to the question.
The Hon. minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is a distinguished gentleman, by whom the judiciary has been honoured. He resides in the Montreal division of St. Anne's, one of the most important as regards trade and manufacture. What is he doing to promote an exhibition in Montreal?

Mr. Ames is a prominent man, a man high in his party, who represents one of the wealthy divisions of Montreal. What is he doing to forward the movement? The late lamented Mr. Monk had inaugurated a scheme of that kind. One day he called together all the farmers around Montreal. I was present and addressed the meeting. For a time I thought success had been achieved; but the usual happened, and the preparations fell through. Is it not pitiful to see Montreal, the queen city of Canada, with its population, manufactures and harbour facilities, without her exhibition. Toronto boasts of a splendid fair; I attend every year; it is both beautiful and instructive. I have seen in the one day an attendance of 300,000 at the Toronto Fair. Ottawa has her national exhibition. I am a regular visitor there too. Beautiful exhibits are to be seen, which are an encouragement, to agriculture and industry. It also records a large attendance. Three Rivers, Sherbrooke and Quebec, as well as the western cities, hold an annual fair. But in Montreal there is no place to put even a cat on exhibition. And yet the queen-city of Canada has among its representatives in this House men of great worth, even ministers; but Montreal in this respect, is completely neglected. Of course farmers are told: Keep to the soil, till the land; but the produce of your labour will not be exhibited. Toil away, spend large amounts to breed good stock, but keep your thoroughbreds in your stables; you have no place to show them. How long will we stand for this state of things? Will not the member for Jacques Cartier take the initiative of the movement, and shake the members of the Government out of their apathy? Could not advantage be taken of some important centenary to have a large exposition at Montreal?
Another cause of dissatisfaction, M'-\ Speaker, lies in the stubborn refusal of the Dominion Government to improve our roads. At first the Government intended to spend a large amount for that purpose and a scheme to that effect was put before the House. But when tne Bill was amended by the Senate, the Government refused to accept the proposed amendment. And yet that amendment was fair and proper. We were in favour of the expenditure of millions for good roads, but we were unwilling that it should be distributed under the control of the Dominion department. The amendment provided for a pro rata parcelling of this credit to the different provinces on the basis of population. And 
this should have been accepted. To do otherwise would have been an infringement of provincial autonomy.
Mr. RAINVILLE i('Translation): The hon. member suggests improvements and pleads for the farmer. He has requested the Dominion Government to enact various measures in the interest of agriculture and to subsidize it in various ways. How is it that, as regards good roads, he is of a different mind and asks that the grants be made through the provinces?
I claim that the Dominion Government should give aid to the farmers, but through the intermediary of the provinces.
Even for the cultivation of tobacco?

The
fiscal regulations governing tobacco come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Inland Revenue. My hon. friend (Mr. Rainville) who represents in this House, as I do myself, the agricultural element of his province, ought to stand by me in the request I have been making.

My answer to the hon. member, and I make it in passing, is that I am most anxious to help the farmers. I wish to say that for three years past, although ,$600,000 have been received by the Quebec Government to promote agriculture, not a cent of that money has been spent in the two counties of Chambly and Verchferes.

If such is the case, it is to be regretted indeed.
Mr. RAINiViILLE (Translation):	If the
Dominion 'Government took unto itself to distribute its grants, I should be delighted.
Mr. (LAFORTUNE (Translation): I contend that after elections a member of Far-liament becomes the representative of all interests. He must look after the welfare of all classes and see to it that they all get equal justice. If favours and privileges are to be bestowed; if, for instance, patronage is to be distributed and government positions filled, it is only good tactics to confer these favours on the recommendation of friends of the Government. It has been the constant practice. It may be an evil, but it has always been the usual thing. But when the welfare of agriculture is at stake, where those great predominating interests are concerned, the white flag is the one to hoist, not the red or the blue.

Merchants have often complained to me of the need for a bankruptcy law. They claim that such a law identical for the whole Dominion is a necessity. Canadian trade to-day is interprovincial. The Montreal tradesmen, through their commercial travellers, deal with Winnipeg, Toronto, the maritime and the western provinces. Those who sell their wares have a right to a uniform bankruptcy Act. But the farmer must be left out of its operation; as he is not a trader, he cannot go into bankruptcy. I realize that in the business of the merchant and the manufacturer, there are fluctuations. Some unforeseen event may happen which forces him to declare his insolvency. He makes a settlement with his creditors, and once peace is restored, he begins anew. Not so with the farmer. If things go ill with him, he is debarred from making a settlement with his creditors; he cannot begin all anew. If a bankruptcy law is enacted, therefore, the farmer should be excepted from its operation. A debt to a farmer is as sacred as are the salaries of employees. Such a law is necessary, and the merchants are urging that it be passed. The Government should give the matter early consideration. For the last two sessions, I brought an important subject to the attention of the ex-Postmaster General, who, unfortunately for me, but perhaps happily for himself, has given up politics for good. I wish to mention the matter to the new Postmaster General. To my mind an enactment is urgently required' forbidding the posting of money letters without prior registration. I always feel sorry, when as Crown Attorney I have to proceed against poor employees of the Post Office Department, who often belong to respectable families; because post office employees are generally sons of members, or of professional men who in order to earn wherewith to complete their studies, seek in the meantime a position in the Post Office Department. Almost every month some of these young men are brought before the courts for having stolen fifty cents or sometimes a dollar, and the minimum sentence is three months at hard labour. Is it not pitiful to see a young man, the son of a judge, a member, or a professional man condemned for such a petty theft? Registered letters are not stolen, because they are easily traced. In France one is not allowed to put a cent in an ordinary envelope under penalty of a fine or imprisonment. Why not do the same thing here? It would cost nothing; on the contrary it would bring some revenue to the Government.
Instead of charging five cents for registration, a three-cent stamp might be sufficient. But in any case no money letter should be mailed without being registered. The ex-Postmaster General had acknowledged the desirability of such a measure. His answer was that, after listening to my plea, he found that the grounds I put forward would justify such an enactment and that he would give me a reply at this session. He is now gone, and, I hope to occupations more congenial to him. The present Postmaster General will, I trust, read the remarks, I have just been making. The post office at Montreal, together with its branches, comprises a large number of employees. Not a week passes but some one of them is brought up who has fallen from grace. His name is kept secret, and, for the sake of his family, the matter is hushed up but he goes to the penitentiary just the same. It is altogether deplorable.
For the last quarter of a -century, no exposition has been held in Montreal. I am the owner of high-priced horses and in order to exhibit them, I should have to ship them to Toronto or Ottawa, there being -no fair held in Montreal. And to think there are in this House ministers who represent Montreal! Let something be done for that city. The Board of Trade, the capitalists, the large hotels, all clamour after an exposition. Meetings without number are held; resolution after resolution is adopted, and yet nothing is accomplished. I urge the ministers to consider earnestly the remarks I have made and see that Montreal gets its exposition. Everywhere exhibitions receive grants. With that I have no fault to find; they are a necessity. But should not Montreal get its share of the public moneys? Montreal is the city which furnishes most to the public treasury. The Canadian metropolis -seems to be the victim of a conspiracy. The farmers are told: you are the -monarchs of this land; the country looks up -to you. But the farmers in turn have a right to look up to the Government. They are interested in this exhibition. Not only should Montreal hold an annual fair, but an international exposition should be organized with permanent buildings, an exposition worthy of this great city's commerce and industries.
Such an exposition should be held at Saint Laurent, in the division of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. Fine, up-to-date buildings should be erected for the purpose at Saint Laurent. There are already to be found in that suburb a college

and a convent; the transportation facilities are many; and as it is the custom at such fairs to have horse races, there are splendid grounds which could be turned into a racetrack. At the Chicago fair college students served as guides to the visitors. I ask the hon. member for Jacques Cartier to give his best consideration to that proposal for an exposition at Montreal.
The continued British embargo on our cattle is also to be deplored. That restriction on Canadian cattle has for some years past prevented its exportation, with a consequent loss to the cattle trade. We are draining our resources to the extent of millions of dollars in order to help the old country. Why, then, should there be discrimination against our cattle, under the pretence that they are not healthy. That embargo should be raised. Why is it allowed to continue ? It is an arbitrary measure. There is no sense or justice in thus depreciating the value of our cattle by alleging that they are infected with tuberculosis. If our herds are contaminated, the fact should be disclosed here previous to shipment, and not after the freight and insurance charges have been paid. It is otherwise a gross injustice. I do not wish to appear too critical of British methods, but I wish to point out that the representations we have made have passed unheeded, and we continue to be ill-treated in that respect. The time has come when a stop must be put to such a state of things.
I said something a while ago about the necessity for a Dominion Insolvency Act. The Ontario Act regarding insolvent debtors is different from that of Quebec, and the latter again is different from the enactments of the maritime provinces on the same subject. Such legisation is asked for by all merchants. An attempt at framing an Act has already been made, and Judge Fortin, then member for Laval, prepared a Bill to that effect; but the House prorogued before the Bill had been put through. Later, in 1902, Mr. Fortin was appointed to the judiciary and the Bill was not again taken up. But Insolvency Acts ought not to include debts due to a farmer, who is not a trader. A merchant can always make a new start; it is the usual thing in trade. But the farmer cannot. His claims should, therefore, be privileged and not be included in the proceedings in bankruptcy.
The interest of the country demands that greater encouragement be given to the cultivation of fruit-trees. A special grant should be apportioned among fruit-growers, and fMr. Lafortune.]
inspectors should be appointed to supervise the improvement of orchards, especially, when they are infested with pests. Of what use is it for a diligent grower to give his trees the best of care if his neighbour, by neglecting to attend to his trees, breeds the pests which will infest the neighbourhood. Special inspectors should be appointed by the Government to see that noxious insects are destroyed. Such a measure is of first importance.
When the Government undertook to guarantee $55,000,000 of bonds of the Canadian Northern railway, I had requested that the company extend its Montreal-Raw-don line to the Transcontinental railway. These millions of dollars were voted after the company had pledged itself to extend its branch lines. In my county there is an important line from Montreal to Rawdon and we had received the assurance from the officials of the company that it would be extended to the Transcontinental. I am sorry to say that nothing has been done so far. The poor settlers of my county should at all costs be helped out of the painful position in which they are now. I (very, specially recommend the extension of this line.
At the last electoral campaign, the discussion between my opponents and myself took place over the expenditure. They alleged that the Liberal ministers had been extravagant spendthrifts; that, in the words of the Minister of Finance, their expenditure had been uncontrolled and uncontrollable. There was some fight also over the navy, and especially in Ontario, over the " ne temere." Laurier was held accountable for mixed marriages. The speech makers also brought in the school question. As mentioned by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, the pledge was given that if the Conservatives were put at the helm of the state, this question would be settled in short order. Reciprocity was also fought for and against, our opponents shouting:	"Let well enough alone." And
then there was the question of prohibition.
I for one am a total abstainer; I make use of neither tobacco nor liquor; but Mr. Laurier, who is himself an abstainer, did not wish to foist prohibition on the province of Quebec and I think he was right. But we hope that at the next election the navy will be out of the debate,-our Conservative friends will not dare introduce the subject-the ne temere will have been buried, the school question will be no more, as Mr. Monk stated, and the reciprocity treaty will not be an issue. How

strange indeed! When we were in power, the members on your left, Mr. Speaker, reproached us saying:	You promised
reciprocity and you have not brought it about; and when it was practically brought about, we were blamed for doing it, and that was one of the causes of the Liberal defeat. The object of these remarks is to lay bare the insincerity of these gentlemen. At the present time, corn is the only feed that we import for our hogs, horses and cows. Corn previously was on the free list, but the present Government has put a duty on the only feed we do not produce.
The exit from the House of the ex-Post-'master General leaves me indifferent. The present minister Hon. T. Chase Casgrain, is a worthy successor; he is an honest man, and a fine orator. I believe he is worthy of the portfolio confided to his care.
Mr. Nantel exclaimed at St. Jerome:	I
will cut off my hand before anything is given to Great Britain; but to-day that gentleman who accused the Liberals of living at the public expense is himself a member of the Railway Commission; he receives a splendid salary and is happy.
The hon. member for Dorchester has also had his reward; he performs his duties of Deputy Speaker in a dignified manner. The hon. membeT for L'lslet will soon be appointed postmaster. I rejoice with him.
In the course of my experience, there is one thing that came particularly to my notice. When, in 1897, I made an investigation officially as Royal Commissioner into the administration of the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, I found that all the prisoners were mixed up without any attempt at classification. The old offenders and the young criminals were all together. These old relapsers are in a sort the teachers of crime for the younger element.
In my capacity as Royal Commissioner, I had recommended to Sir Oliver Mowat, the then Minister of Justice, that the prisoners be put in three classes. The recommendation was to be carried out, but the thing was not done. If the hon. the Minister of Justice could only realize the evils attendant on the present system, he would without delay establish a system of classification, whereby the old criminals would be put in a room apart and the younger men in their own separate quarters. Why should they be left together to eat, to go to church, etc.? They ought to be separated. Such a reform is most desirable. The life prisoners are very dangerous men. Their sole thought is to find a means of escape; all
their life, they go on plotting and conspiring. A serious evil exists, and the only remedy is the proper classification of criminals.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member must be aware that the question before the House is the only question to which he can properly direct his attention. This debate has gone on with considerable latitude, and I have not attempted to restrict it in any way; but it does seem to me, after listening for quite a long time to a discussion of the affairs of the country, that the matter of the classification of criminals is not pertinent to the question before the House, which is as follows :
That this House is ready to provide for the exigencies of the present situation and to vote all necessary ways and means to that end, but it regrets that in the measure under consideration duties are imposed which must be oppressive upon the people whilst yielding little or no revenue, and that the said measure is particularly objectionable in the fact that instead of favouring, it is placing extra barriers against Great Britain's trade with Canada, at a moment when the Mother Country is under a war strain unparalleled in history.
That is the question which stands for the consideration and decision of the House, and it is the only one to which the hon. gentleman can properly direct his attention in this debate. I am reluctant to draw the hon. members attention to the matter, but I thought that, being a comparatively new member, he was not, perhaps, as familiar with the rule as older members of the House are.
I was trying to show that the Government should effect some remedy in the matter of the classification of criminals. That is the point I was discussing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is a point which is not pertinent to the question under consideration. The matter before the House refers not to criminals, criminology or criminal classification, but to the question of duties.

I comply with your decision, Mr. Speaker, and I pass to another question.
I have referred already to the schools and I say that instead of voting millions to help Great Britain, we should not lose sight of our duty towards our compatriots in Ontario. I do not find fault with the legitimate expenditure of millions of dollars, but I say that we should endeavour, by all possible means, to help in the settlement of the difficulties which divide British subjects in Ontario. The question of schools is one of language. That the Government

should keep in mind. If millions have to he spent for the war, I agree to it, but I add that something should be done towards settling that vexed question.
May I ask the hon. member how the Government *could bring about the settlement of that difficulty.

By taking steps to nave it determined whether the provincial government had the right to do as it has done. These gentlemen on your right, Mr, Speaker, could give the same pledge they have given when they were in opposition. The question is identical to that raised by the member for Jacques Cartier regarding the Manitoba schools.
The Government's programme, as expounded in the Speech from the throne, insists on the necessity for the farmers to remain on the farms and till the soil. That is a very commendable policy and one with which I am in thorough sympathy. But the Government, by way of encouragement, cuts down the number of representatives for the rural districts to increase the representation of cities. A strange encouragement, indeed! The farmers are told to till the soil and in return the protection to which they are entitled is taken away from them. In the cities the citizens have easy access to their representatives; indeed two hours riding In an automobile will enable one to make a complete survey of a city electoral division. An urban elector is in contact with the whole world. The newspaper brings the news of the universe to his breakfast table. In the country, on the other hand, miles and miles have to be travelled over and, as the hon. member for Terrebonne must have experienced, the roads are not always of the best.
So great was the country's prosperity under Liberal rule, that money was flowing everywhere, and the rate of interest had to be lowered from six to five per cent. Legislation had also to be enacted against usury. To the Liberals also is due credit for having introduced the secret ballot. The member for Jacques Cartier claims for his party the credit of having made Canada what it is. That is no small pretension. The Conservative majority did not see to safeguarding the small borrowers against the evils of usury. Under the Conservative rule, industries decline, while the good Liberal Administration made them thrive. With the Liberals in power, the workingmen were prosperous, in fact prosperity was general. Laurier promoted a healthy 
immigration, and guided by his wise policy the settlement of the country made immense strides. Many sons and daughters of Canada who had left for the United States have returned. Expatriation to the United States was the consequence of Conservative administration. It stopped during the Liberal rule.
My last word is that it was well that Sir Wilfrid Laurier should be defeated that he might be spared the responsibility of what is now going on and of the mistakes which are being committed. But his time will come and history will record that he was the greatest among the great. He will restore to Canada that great prosperity which it enjoyed under his Government.
I beg to thank my hon. fellow-members who have listened to my remarks with so much respect and attention. Such consideration is gratifying to one who addresses the House.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I would be remiss in the duty which I owe to the electors in the constituency which I have the honour to represent if I did not make a few remarks in connection with the subject which is now under consideration.
In the first place, I would like to compliment the right hon. leader of the Government and his ministers upon the splendid manner in which they have transacted the business of the country, especially since war was declared. I feel that in attending to the affairs of state they have given their untiring efforts to the accomplishment of that which is in the best interests of the whole people of Canada. The manner in which the right hon. leader of the Government has taken charge of the business of the country has tended to endear him still further, if possible, to the people, who are at all times glad to bestow upon him the honour of being one of the greatest statesmen and leaders that the Dominion of Canada has ever produced. I wish also to commend the hon. Minister of Finance for the splendid manner in which he laid his Budget before the House and for the matter contained in his Budget speech.
I feel that the hon. Minister of Finance did credit not only to himself tout also to the people who are supporters of the party to which we are glad he belongs at this particular time.
I am sure that I do not owe the House any apology for not attempting to reply to the speech of the last speaker (Mr. Lafortune), but I wish to make just a passing

reference to one or two of the utterances of the speaker who preceded him (Mr. J. J. Hughes). I was surprised to hear the hon. member attempt to liken the doings of the Finance Minister in connection with his expenditures to the actions of a drunken sailor. The hon. member stated, I think, that the Government owed an apology, not only to a drunken sailor, but to a shipload of drunken sailors. His remarks in this connection remind me of an incident that took place in the province of Ontario some years ago. On one occasion the Liberal party, who were in power at that time, were asked for an apology for the actions not merely of one drunken sailor, hut of a shipload of drunken sailors who were landed at a certain point in the province of Ontario. According to the information which I have received, and which has been spread broadcast throughout the province of Ontario, these sailors did not belong to the party which occupy the Government benches in the House of Commons at the present . time. In case the hon. gentleman, who is not now in his seat, should take the trouble to look the matter up with a view to refuting these statements, I am glad to be able to refer him to the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) or to the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Smythe) or to the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce). If he wants any further information about the actions of any government whose doings may well be likened to the actions of a drunken sailor, I think he may obtain all the information he wants from the hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred.
Many allusions have been made to the patriotism of the people throughout the Dominion of Canada. I feel that the greatest credit is due to the people of Canada for the splendid way in which they have responded to the call of the Empire for assistance in this time of great trial. I can speak only for the people in my own immediate vicinity, in the county in which I live, and in the adjoining portions of the province of Ontario; but I am delighted to tell members of this House, regardless of the party to which they may belong or the part of the country from which they may come, that the response of a patriotic nature has been a credit to every person who happens to live in that portion of the province.
A number of members of the Opposition
raised a great deal of objection to and criticism of the arrangement of the tariff under the administration of the Government and the Minister of Finance. Some of them seemed to be forced to express biased opinions to suit the different parts of the Dominion in which they happen to reside. As a new member of the House, I do not wish any members of the Opposition to infer that I would endeavour to make an unjust or unfair criticism of their comments on the Budget and the tariff. But I cannot avoid contrasting the feeling shown by the hon. member for South Bruce (Mr. Truax) and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), both Opposition members, both members of the Government .and both personal friends of mine, neither of whom have I ever heard say anything that was not quite agreeable to the Government's policy of protection, with the befuddled dreams and delusions of free trade uttered by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). It must, Sir, be a severe strain on your patience to have to listen to the speeches which are delivered by Opposition members in criticism of the Government's tariff policy. To hear their speeches one would suppose there yvas not unanimity upon this side of the House on tariff matters. From my own observation, and from listening to the speeches which have been delivered in the Budget debate, I am forced to the conclusion that there is a great deal more unanimity upon the tariff question on the Government side than we find on the Opposition side. We find a good deal of opposition to the increased customs duties. Personally, having recently been in western Ontario, I found that very little criticism was offered in the country upon the increase of 71 per cent.
Some of the Opposition members argue that the increase is not going to be effective in raising revenue. Possibly that is so; but whether or not it is going to be immediately effective in raising revenue, which everybody admits is absolutely necessary for the war expenditure, I think it is going to be eventually effective. In support of this I may say that the increased duty on goods coming in from foreign countries, especially from the United States, has had the effect of putting a crimp in the manufacturers over there to the extent that some of them have already felt it was in their own interest to come to different cities in Canada and manufacture articles which they had previously manufactured in the United States and exported to Canada. I am sorry that the bon. member for-South Wellington is not present, because I am sure he could substantiate my statements, as already there

has been established in the city of Guelph where he lives a factory for the manufacture of articles that have never before been manufactured in Canada. 'It makes no difference to the financial standing of the people of Canada whether they receive the . money in duties collected at the border ports on goods coming in or whether the arrangement of the tariff is sufficiently protective to force American firms to come here and manufacture, I claim that in the city of Guelph and in the county where I live the fact of that concern being forced to come there and open operations to manufacture the goods used in Canada, for which they admit they have had a very large trade for their factories in the United States, will lead to the opening of similar institutions in other cities, that will bring in people and put in circulation money that will be required to carry on these industries, and in some way will have the same effect on the Dominion of Canada, directly or indirectly, as if the revenue had been collected at the border in the shape of customs taxes.
I wish to refer briefly to some speeches that have- been delivered by western members, although I might confine my remarks to Alberta and Saskatachewan. Sometimes I can hardly make myself believe the remarks of the hon. members from those districts when they depict the situation there financially and in every other way as deplorable.
We are glad that those who have migrated from Ontario and the eastern provinces have gone to the West, and I am sure that the people in the East will always do what they feel they should do in the interests of the people of the West. But the members from the western provinces would like to lead this House to believe that the present Government is to blame for the money stringency in the West. I for one am not prepared to admit that that is the case. I believe that this condition of affairs is due to many reasons, which it is not necessary for me to explain here, but everybody knows a few of them; for instance, the speculative' madness, the over valuation of real estate, and things of that kind.
I feel perfectly satisfied that legislation could be put on the statute books by this Parliament which would be in the interests of those provinces at a time when they need it, but I am not prepared to stand for the remarks of the members of the West who try to make us believe that the present condition of affairs out there is wholly due to the action of the Government. I remember hearing the Minister of Finance, 
shortly after the Conservative party took the reins of office, make the statement during a discussion with reference to the banking affairs of the provinces to which I have referred, that the financial condition of those provinces was not very flourishing. He stated that there was 40 per cent more money on loan than on deposit in Alberta and Saskatchewan at that time. In view of the conditions confronting this Government when they came into power, and of the conditions brought about by the war, I do not think it is fair for the western members to blame the Government for the present condition of the country.
We hear a great deal at the present time about the patriotism-and-production meetings that are being held throughout the Dominion. I quite -agree with the holding of such meetings. I think they are beneficial to the country, although I think they are hardly necessary in the central and western portions of Ontario, for the farmers in that part of the country realize that it i>s in their own interest to produce the greatest possible amount of foodstuffs; -and they are doing so.
I am quite willing to admit that the people in the West may have grievances at the present time, but I am sure the Government is willing to assist the people in that part of the country and in the whole Dominion to the best of their power. But we are never willing to admit that it would have been in the interests of my part of the Dominion of Canada to have had come into effect the trade agreements that were presented to the country by the Liberal party in the election of 1911. I believe that the policy of the Conservative party will be much more in the interests of the Dominion as a whole.
1 again wish to compliment the Minister of Finance for having made what I consider to be the best regulation of the tariff possible under the circumstances. I feel sure that the people of this country, so far from criticising the Government, will approve of the proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance, and will certainly not agree with those members who have taken what might be called an over-zealous part, if they have not put up even a little bit of obstruction.

Mr. Speaker, at this late hour of the night, I believe you do not expect that I shall make a very lengthly speech upon the question which to-day is under discussion in this House and stirs the electorate of the country. But, as representative of an essentially agricultural county, I think it my duty, notwithstanding the lateness of

the hour, to claim the attention of the House a few moments, in order to expound, Mr. Speaker, my opinion and my views on the subject which we are called upon to consider just now.
The member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) has deemed it profitable for this House and for the whole of Canada to make known to us his particular views regarding the problems about which the electors are presently concerned. In fervid thought subdued tones, he informed us that the Right Hon. the Prime Minister is a great admirer of the Catholic faith and a close student of the French language; and appealing to those dispositions in the Prime Minister, unappreciated until to-day, he requested him to exercise his influence to obtain a settlement of the bi-lingual school question in Ontario. Really, Mr. Speaker, a better statement was expected from the hon. member of his stand on the subject which has absorbed the thoughts of this House for the last few days. What does he think of the new taxes laid on the people for the purpose of raising funds for Canada's contribution to the defence of the Empire, as is claimed by the Minister of Finance? What stand does he take on this mode of participation in Imperial wars? It seems to me that his former declarations, particularly those he made publicly in 1910, during the electoral campaign of Drummond and Arthabaska, should have left some recollection of certain statements contained in the speeches he made at the time. But, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must have found his road to Damascus on the way to the sugar bush, and especially since the time he took his seat at your right and enjoys Government patronage. He has found out, Mr. Speaker, that he made a mistake two years ago, when he placed Cartier's cloak on Hon. L. P. Pelletier's shoulders. For the time being he takes it and places it on the shoulders of the hon. the Postmaster General. Let us hope that the minister will not find it too heavy. It is not without interest, Mr. Speaker, to consider at leisure the changes that are wrought, sometimes within a brief period, in the minds of certain men. Those who have heard the speeches delivered by the hon. member for L'lslet before and during the elections of 1911, will no doubt wonder as to whether he is the same man who had been addressing this House. In any case, I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for L'Islet will not beseech the present Postmaster General, as he has his predecessor, Mr. Pelletier, to make Confederation fruitful. I think I speak rightly, Mr. Speaker, when I state that the political
truce which we of the Liberal party have scrupulously kept since the declaration of war of the 4th August last, has been broken by our friends on the other side of the House, who have given free expression to their partisanship. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) was the first to communicate to this House his illusions and to open a discussion on the most acute phase of politics. So, at page 493 of this session's unrevised edition of Hansard, we find the following pronouncement by this gentleman:
The next week, however, it was cabled to Canada from England that the trade routes were perfectly safe, and that the people of this country could export their produce as usual. What was it that made the trade routes safe? The British fleet For years, every other overseas dominion had been contributing to the upkeep of that fleet. But the supremacy of Britain on the seas meant more to Canada, and particularly to the farmers of Canada, than it did to the people of any, or perhaps all, of the other overseas dominions; and yet this country, because of the action of the hon. gentlemen opposite, was in the position of being the only one of the overseas dominions that had never contributed a cent towards maintaining the supremacy of the British navy.
(Translation):	The hon. member for
Lambton East (Mr. Armstrong) alluded to the same question in his speech which is reported in pages 622 and 623 of this session's unrevised edition of Hansard. Here are his words:
And more than that, they were able to assist Admiral Beatty in the splendid victory he achieved in the North Sea. The cry with these gentlemen opposite was, no need; no danger; no emergency; no menace; we know what we are talking about and there is no need for the Government to undertake this proposition. But the Premier had asked the British Admiralty how he could best serve them in that regard, and he is asking them to-day. This Government to-day are carrying out the wishes of the British Admiralty, and we fare proud and glad to support them. But hon. gentlemen opposite are doing their utmost to discredit this Government in the eyes of Canada and the world at large, and if possible drive them to the country. We on this side of the House feel proud and glad that we have at the head of affairs in Canada such an honest, straight-forward and businesslike Government, a Government which from time to time gives to the people of Canada pieces of legislation as progressive as could possibly be expected from any Government.
'When the House rose at six o'clock I was calling attention to the fact that the Government had obeyed the wishes of the British Admiralty in 1911 and, had their policy not been thwarted in this House and defeated in the Senate by the Liberal party, Canada and Great Britain would to-day have been much better prepared for this war. Upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen opposite, therefore, rests a great responsibility, and when called upon to give an

account of their stewardship in the near future, they will cut a sorry figure before the people, when they have to tell them that their policy in this House so far this session has been to embarrass and hinder the Government in promoting the necessary legislation to help the Empire to bring this great struggle to a successful issue. When war broke out we had no great dreadnoughts to place in the firing line, and for that hon. gentlemen opposite are to Name. They do not dare to vote in opposition to the $100,000,000 asked for by the Government now, nor did they dare to vote last summer against the $50,000,000 for war expenditure, but they do dare to try their utmost to embarrass and obstruct and criticise the necessary legislation. The Government now in power have done their full duty in this crisis. One hundred thousand of our brave sons have been armed and equipped and fed, and great credit is due to the men at the head of affairs who have been so successful in this undertaking. Apparently hon. gentlemen opposite are now taking up the time of Parliament with the object of driving the Government to the country, and if that be their wish, and if the Government should appeal to the country, these hon. gentlemen must expect very little sympathy from the electorate. Look at what the colonies are doing in this great war; see the splendid work of Australia!
Hear, hear.

Will hon. gentlemen opposite pound their desks when I remind them of the attitude taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, in 1902, 1907, and 1909* before the Colonial Conferences? When he was asked at these conferences to subscribe to the assistance of the British navy and the defence of the British Empire the attitude taken by him was in direct opposition to the best interests of the people of Canada at that time, and while Australia and New Zealand were willing to subscribe from year to year towards the maintenance of the British navy, and towards assisting in the defence of the Empire.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to read the minds of the twenty-two colleagues of the hon. member for Lambton, who hail from the province of Quebec, and sit with him in this House. These gentlemen, during the last general elections, swooped down upon the parishes of the province of Quebec and denounced the Liberals who had decided upon the building of a Canadian navy designed in case of need to defend the interests of Canadian trade. If Canada's unpreparedness at the < opening of hostilities was such as depicted by the hon. member for Lambton, whose fault is it? If for a whole month our trade, at least that which happened to be in our harbours, was held up, who is responsible? Are not the guilty ones to be found among those who sit on your right to-day? are they not those gentlemen who at the time of the passing of the Naval Act in 1910, and from that day on, until after the elections of 1911, have made the most unfair campaign ever witnessed. The hon. member for Lambton 
complains bitterly of our attitude and that of the Senate during the session of 1913, regarding the proposal to contribute $35,000,000 to the British navy. That policy was assailed by the Liberal party. My friend and I fought against it and I should still oppose it were it again submitted to us. I am quite ready to go back to my constituency and submit to my electors my stand on this question; and I do not believe that a single member on this side of the House entertains any fears for his reelection on that issue. The present war has demonstrated beyond a doubt that the British navy is well able not only to take care of itself hut to give help to its allies. It is made clear to-day that Great Britain can without any contribution on our part maintain its supremacy on the seas, since she has succeeded in establishing the blockade of the North Sea, of the British Channel, and of a part of the Mediterranean. For my part, I am still convinced that the only judicious naval policy for Canada, is that put forth by the Liberal party. From the speech of the hon. member for Lambton East, one would gather, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberals have been at the helm of state from Confederation to 1911. It is common history, however, that throughout the whole time from 1867 to 1896, four years only, from 1874 to 1878, came under Liberal rule. How comes that during those twenty-five years the Conservatives never thought of making such a contribution to the Imperial navy? The reason, Mr. Speaker, is to be found in that there was at the time at the head of the Conservative party men who understood the underlying principles of our constitution, men such as are to be found to-day at the head of the Lioeral party. I mean that the then leaders of the Conservative phalanx, held as do the present Liberal leaders, that what was needed at the time, and what is needed to-day, is not a policy of contribution but a policy of organization. The Liberals, Mr. Speaker, have every reason to be proud of the stand taken by them in 1909 and 1910; they may also be proud of the electoral campaign of 1911. On this question, if ever an opportunity can be given the people to realize the error they have made in withdrawing the reins of government from an Administration which has secured for the country happiness, prosperity and peace, this opportunity is to he be found in the present war. In fact, everybody admits to-day that the naval policy of the Liberal party is the only true Canadian policy, the only policy that fits in with our national interests.
Let us now discuss another subject. There

is submitted to our consideration the resolution of the Minister of Finance, upon the ways and means to secure the money required to meet our present obligations and provide for those that are to arise. It is argued, Mr. Speaker, that our present financial situation is the consequence of the war and the new taxation to be levied upon the people has been christened war taxes. I maintain that this view is a false one, and I may point out from the admissions of the Minister of Finance himself that there is no foundation to it, because the minister has declared that all the money necessary for the war will be borrowed from the British Government. It then follows that we are not called upon at the present time to provide for this war. The truth of it is made more apparent when from the speech of the Minister of Finance there come out plain and manifest the real motives of this taxation. The true causes of the new imposts are that during the fiscal year ending the 31st instant the revenue of the country has diminished and the expenditure has increased to such an extent that during the year a deficit of 60 millions of dollars has accumulated in the management of the current business of the country, and this without taking into account the 50 millions voted last August for the defence of Canada and the Empire. The administration, Mr. Speaker, has been improvident; too much has been spent thoughtlessly; this it is that brought about the alarming conditions in which the Government finds itself to-day. But are those gentlemen sitting on the Treasury benches willing to better the situation? What are their intentions for the year commencing on the 1st of April next? The Minister of Finance states that he expects during the coming year a revenue of 120 millions of dollars. How is that to be spent? 140 millions will go to cover the ordinary expenditure and 50 millions will be entered to capital account. Was that to be expected from the Government? Is that the course that an ordinary business man would take in a similar position? I think I may state, without fear of contradiction, that not another man outside of those included in the present Government would act in such a way. And do not lose sight of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that this deficit of 60 millions of dollars for the current year, and next year's anticipated of 70 to 80 millions do not comprise any of the 150 millions of dollars voted for the war.
