Really, the situation is far from encouraging; but it is not without remedy. It is possible to
restore the equilibrium in the finances, but energy is required; useless expenses must be cut down; and all expenditure which is not absolutely urgent should be postponed to a later date. Thus, the Government could make a saving of many millions of dollars in reducing the civil service list; public works could be left for later consideration where there is no urgency for them, such works as 'drill halls and post offices in small localities; the construction of the Hudson Bay Railway could wait, as could also many other public undertakings too numerous to mention. The Government has spent recklessly, its duty is to apply the cure. I wish to remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that during Liberal rule, the country has also known days of stress, but the Government of the day, composed of men of energy, bent on protecting the people's welfare, has been able to weather the storm, sail through the different phases of the crisis without taxing the people for a single cent.
If the present Government had kept the ordinary expenditure at the same figure that it was in 1911, when it came into power, and it could if it would, it would not now have to face the sad necessity of imposing taxes on the people to meet the current expenditure of administration. Unfortunately, the Government lacks energy and the sense of economy, so that little hope can be entertained for the relief of the people. Since the new Administration has taken hold of power, there has been witnessed a shameless squandering of the public money. The Civil Service list has increased from five to eight millions of dollars, through the unnecessary appointment of employees who were not in any way required. There is paid in rent only for housing the employees $175,000 a year; besides what had to be paid to furnish these new offices, put in telephones, appoint caretakers, etc., etc. Will any one fairly pretend that 10,000 additional employees were required since 1911? The people will never believe it. How is it, Mr. Speaker, that it was possible for the Liberal Government, during a time of unprecedented prosperity, to administer the public affairs with 10,000 employees less than at present.
It is not my desire to enter into all the details of the management and wasting methods of the present Government; it would take too long. I will only mention that when we of the Liberal party spent at most 79 to 98 millions of dollars in one year, we had sufficient revenue to meet the expenditure, with fair surplus at that with-

out having to impose additional burdens on the people.
This, Mr. Speaker, brings me to the new taxes. What remedy is proposed by the Minister of Finance to improve the present situation? In the first place, an increase of 1\ per cent of the general tariff and 5 per cent of the preferential. This increase is expected to yield a large sum. But, Mr. Speaker, the question frames itself: If that sum is secured at whose expense will it be? Is it not the people and especially the farmers, because such increased tax spells higher prices for agricultural implements. They will also have to pay more for the goods they have to buy. Is the Minister of Finance aware that a general increase in prices has taken place since August last, that many classes of goods have disappeared entirely from the market and cannot be had, and that this state of affairs will last so long as the north of France and Belgium are not replenished and their manufactures put on the same footing as before the war. Of what good then is this duty of 7J per cent on goods that cannot be imported? So that increase in the tariff will not provide the expected revenue. On the other hand, the higher duties will mean new difficulties and still higher prices. No, Mr. Speaker, the solution offered by the Minister of Finance is not the one suitable to solve the difficulties which have arisen consequent on the Government's negligence.
But from my point of view the most bitter medicine to swallow is the direct taxation with which the Minister of Finance proposes to burden the people. In the first place, one per cent is to be collected on banking transactions. Is it your belief, Mr. Speaker, that the banks will have to bear that burden? No, indeed; the banks will get it back by increasing the rate of discount and once again the poor will pay for the rich. The minister told us the other day that to meet this tax the Bank of Montreal will have to pay $150,000 a year and the Canadian Bank of Commerce $175,000 and so the other banks, according to the sum total of the business done. Not the banks will pay that tax but the people. Take for instance the Canadian Bank of Commerce, which has a branch ,at Acton Vale, my home town; they will increase their discount so as to meet that requirement, and the clients will have to bear the loss. The banks will charge 8 or 9 per cent and perhaps more in order to recoup themselves of the outlay, which they will not pay out of their current revenue.

Now what about the railway tickets? What about the imposition of 5 cents on every ticket above $1? As the leader of the Opposition pointed out, such a tax is unequal and unfair and besides difficult to control. How can the Government collect such a tax on a ticket bought on the train?
The taxes on cheques, bank receipts, bank drafts, etc., etc., are impositions on the people, absolutely useless and burdensome. Take the employees of railway and industrial companies who are paid their salary by cheques; every month they will have to pay this tax. And why? In order to provide the Government with funds to carry on its extravagant expenditure.
The surtax of 50 per cent on letters and 100 per cent on post-card is not warranted. I was listening to the hon. member for Lambton East boasting and praising the Government for having started the rural mail delivery throughout Canada. I'would have no fault to find with that expenditure if the Government were in a position to make it; but I believe that the electors would have preferred to be deprived of the rural mail delivery and not be surtaxed. It is claimed, Mr. Speaker, that this additional stamp will be paid chiefly by the larger trade. This surmise is wrong. The higher trade makes a strict computation of all its outlay before determining the price of its merchandise, in order to realize a certain fixed profit. Everything is taken account of. Ho you imagine that this tax will be left out of the computation. The wholesale merchant will be careful to see that the additional stamps are paid by the purchaser; he will raise his prices and ultimately the one who will pay will be poor consumer.
The same is the case with respect to the patent medicines on which a surtax is laid. Here again those who will suffer are the needy. I am justified in stating that the new taxation is exorbitant and unreasonable. And the same with all the imposts which in the end always fall upon the shoulders of the largest number, and as in this country the working people and the farmers from the largest portion of the population, they it is who will have to bear the new burden.
For all the reasons I have enumerated, I shall vote for the amendment of the hon. the leader of the Opposition and against the scheme of taxation proposed by the Minister of Finance.
I shall then vote for the amendment, because I sincerely believe that the increased tariff is not designed to provide revenue

but for the sole and exaggerated protection of the manufacturers; I shall vote in favour of the amendment because I sincerely believe that the so-called war taxes are a mere pretext with which to deceive the people of Canada, that they are burdensome and their imposition unnecessary. I shall vote for the amendment because I sincerely believe that an Administration honest, energetic and fully realizing the present situation, could meet the country's obligations without imposing any surtax on the Canadian people.
